If you're really into the idea of this game, you'd be better off with the mobile version. It's not written any better but it's more immersive. Some of the crappy jump-scares might actually get to you for a about 2 seconds that way.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

Incredibly disappointing. Started out with a lot of promise, but quickly dove into a linear, absolutely silly plot that doesn't deserve a second play-through. Nothing you do actually matters except for the bearing it has on the last conversation of the game. Wish you could change one response? Too bad, restart the entire game. Excited to experience a different ending? Do EXACTLY the same thing for 3 straight hours but make one different decision to get a different ending.

Text has so many misspellings I couldn't keep track. Voice-overs are rare but still manage to not match the text on screen or mispronounce words completely. Lazy effort all around.

There is so much that could have gone right with this game, but it ended up being a mediocre visual novel with a nonsensical plot, very little character development, and an overall feeling of "wow, what a waste of time."

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a "found phone" psychological mystery / horror game where your curiosity has gotten you involved with a mystery... You found this phone on your doorstep. You initially have no idea what to enter, then the phone glitched and revealed its passcode. You find chat logs, call logs, and the owner was Anna. There was a corrupted video where a terrified Anna screamed that don't come after her... Then the message was cut off. 

As you scan the phone's various steps for clues, and maybe even engage in some social engineering with Anna's friends, including (ex-?) boyfriend Greg, bestie Ashley, and dating app date Taylor, you need to reconstruct Anna's life before she went missing, to have a chance at finding out what happened to her...  

The videos are very high quality, but the simulated phone calls don't sound nearly as good. 

The special effects where the phone glitched got the definitely horror feel to it. Same with the time-warp feel when the phone really glitches out. 

The puzzles such as the sentence scramble and photo scramble doesn't quite fit into the gameplay though.  The "sentence scramble" feels a bit of "make work". Same with the photo scramble. 

There seems to be a lot of alternative paths one can take, so there would be a lot of additional achievements should you want a replay or two. 

All puzzles have clues accessible within the phone itself, though some may be more obscure than others. Part of the fun is to figure out the rest. And there are a lot of red herrings. 

All in all, interesting mechanic for a puzzle game and gradual revelation, if you dig this sort of game.

A unique take on the "found footage" movie style, Simulacra brings that gritty realistic horror to a video game.

There is a voyeuristic thrill that comes with digging though someone else's phone - their photos, their e-mail, even their dating profile - but with the phone's owner in danger and time running out, it becomes a desperate search for the answers that will help you save a woman's life.

If you're looking for a fresh, unique, "thinking outside the box| kind of game, Simulacra delivers.

review_text_raw:
I absolutely love investigative games, and this genre of phone snooping feels especially satisfying to play. Outside of the 'less-than-Oscar-worthy' acting, and the numerous grammatical errors (they're a small southeast Asia company, cut them some slack), SIMULACRA is a very engaging game with an interesting story to tell, focusing on a missing woman named Anna.

I loved being able to figure things out on my own, using the different apps and conversations to piece together where I should go next. I often found myself getting into the headspace of the person that found the phone, because many of the conversations felt as though I was actually speaking to another person. The ending(s) were a little lackluster, but they did the job.


I'm sad that I slept this long on Simulacra, because it really is a fun experience. I just started the second game, and I'm even more invested!

[h1] Review [/h1]
Normally I would write an overly wordy review, but I don't really feel the need here. You want some fun horror, with a fairly innovative premise, that uses the medium of video games in a creative manner? Pick this one up, it's short, it's sweet, though having played some other games of this type, it's definetly not my favorite or anything like that. But it does play with some interesting themes.

Overall, nice horror game where you try to find a girl who has gone missing, through a phone, which has been mysteriously delivered to your doorstep. As always in "these" sorts of games, nothing is completely as it seems.

P.S. The VA is fairly amateurish, but the writing is nice and at the end of the day everyone tried their best, so if you can stomach some mediocre VA, pick this up for sure!

[h3]Cheers for everyone on the acting team, Kaigan Games OÜ and Neon Doctrine, for sharing their art with us, warts and all![/h3]

review_text_raw:
I don't know what qualities I should look for when reviewing horror games, but as someone who has been keen on horror games since childhood, I really enjoyed the game.
Jump-scares are unexpected and frightening, but it was the distorted faces and voices in the glitched videos that really struck me as "scary."

As for the points I don't like:
•Acting sucks. There were scenes that I cringed a lot while watching. Even the text messages are cringe... Like, there are literally missing people out there, and yet everyone uses weird emojis in every damn message.
•As someone who loves choice-based games, only a few of your choices affect the ending, and the game has only 4 different endings (which is way less than I expected.)
•I don't want to spoil the endings, but I must say, I didn't like any of them.
•The phone interface is not good. Its functionality is pretty limited. Chatting is slow, you can't switch between tabs; you can't use the tab button on the keyboard to switch between text boxes, and you can't start videos from a certain timestamp.

Other than these, it's definitely a fun and spooky experience. The price is totally acceptable for 5 hours (and multiple playthroughs with a new game+ / fast chatting mode), so I recommend it.

review_text_raw:
It has its moments. You're interacting with a girl's phone to try and find out what's happened to her. A fun idea for a mystery game, I thought.  At first the game seems to invite you to try to play ethically, meaning, don't lie to any of her contacts. I tried that but then discovered I was failing certain objectives. You're supposed to lie to achieve the intended good outcomes of the game. But before I understood that, when I was trying to play being as honest as possible, I felt like I was being forced to make certain unethical choices. Since I felt like I was being railroaded, I just started doing ridiculous stuff, which led to the game's bad ending. So, on the plus side, my choices really did have consequences. But the problem is the developers' intentions were unclear. I wish I'd known at the beginning of the game what I now understand to be failure and success according to the game's system. I would have enjoyed it a lot more.

The game has a horror element, which is mainly just cheap jump scares. I wouldn't mind them so much if they hadn't mixed the audio so that the jump scare moments are twice as loud as the rest of the game. It's not scary; it's just annoying. I kept having to adjust the volume up and down to avoid the speakers blasting. They ask you to wear headphones because they want the sound to blast in your ears, I guess. There were a few times when the horror was genuinely earned as a result of caring for the characters and a growing understanding of what was at stake, helped along by a few subtle effects. Those were good times...

There's some fun commentary on the inevitable erasure of life as we know it through globalized tech, transhumanism, and 4IR. The fake cyber attack and the resulting driver's license for the internet is the next step, folks! ( ๑ ᴖ ᴈ ᴖ)★

An inventive game I will probably never play again.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a visual novel with some minor horror elements told through a phone.

The basic story is woman goes missing and you end up with her phone. You go through it opening apps, texts, emails, etc, attempting to track her down.

The gameplay is divided into 2 main sections. The first is texting back and forth with people in her text/dating apps. The 2nd section is puzzle based where you need to find/figure out some piece of information to proceed. The game gives you little hints in what you should currently be looking for.

On the plus side: There's some branching paths in response choices that can lead to amusing things happening with various characters. It has multiple endings. Puzzles are actually fairly decent. There're some easter eggs/other things you can mess around with and be amused by.

Looking at the downsides of this: Once you have the whole picture of what's going on, the plot and parts of the story don't make much sense in how they would've play out. The characters aren't that good and one of them is written to be unlikable. Occasionally you'll get video messages and the acting certainly isn't good. Occasional misspellings or responses that don't make much sense. The horror element is more of a background thing, so don't expect it to stand out and be prevalent throughout.

Overall, it's a decent visual novel with some options to fool around with. It's not exceptional in any way, but it's different than standard VRs and has some actual gameplay elements to it, which is nice.

tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

review_text_raw:
This was certainly a unique idea for the game: figuring out what happened to the owner of the phone you picked up by going through the history of her chats and speaking to people on her contact list. The puzzles are intuitive and the game doesn't hold your hand in solving them, so its very satisfying when you get that "EUREKA!" moment as you remember a detail mentioned off-handledy in one of the documents you read hours later.

Yes, the gameplay is thrilling, but I wish it was attached to a more interesting plot. Anna's personal life amounts to standard relationship problems, which wouldn't be such a problem if the characters were more interesting. A troubled girl... her cheating boyfreiend... her supportive friends... and a jokester. All standard horror-movie players and despite games attempts to give them some depth, they just weren't all that engaging. 

There's also the obligatory twist ending. The game does good job building up the mystery and tension of what happened to Anna... but the resolution is rather silly. In general for a horror game its not particularly scary as it mostly relies on predictable jump scares.

Despite the basic premise, the game is quite lengthy (my first playthrough was over 4 houts long) and there's a a bit of replay value to it as some puzzles have several ways to solve depending on what plot choices you make.

7/10 (Mostly for the gameplay and presentation)

review_text_raw:
Basically "Black Mirror: The Game," which can be a good thing if that's what you're into. It's an interesting premise and I respect them for trying something different, but they fall into the same trap that Black Mirror does: saying "technology is bad!" and hammering that idea home over and over and over for hours gets boring after a while.

Within the first ten minutes, the game does a good job establishing the theme of "Technology connects us but leaves us feeling alone." The problem is that once it does that, it doesn't really know where to go from there. There's no meditation on what we as a society can do to work on this, or explorations of how one can learn to find self-worth in such a shallow world. It's just a repeating loop of talking to online dating matches (all losers and jerks), going through Anna's browsing history (all online shopping and personality quizzes), and texting her ex-bf, who's verbally abusive and cheated on her when they were dating. We get an occasional break when we go through her emails, where we learn that she keeps getting rejected from vet school, her boss is unappreciative, and her co-worker is constantly harassing her.

It's all so...bleak, which is fine, but there's just no point to any of it. Like, okay, I get it, the internet sucks and is making us all act like terrible people, but *what's your point*? Should we do something about it? Or just accept it? 

The gameplay is engaging but not very complex, meaning this game relies on its story, which just didn't have enough depth for me. Maybe it's my own fault for being more optimistic about the state of the world, idk, I was just hoping for a story with something more to say other than "phones bad, am i right?"

review_text_raw:
A decent enough experience!
The story revolves around the player who receives a phone by a missing girl by the name of Anna and you  must figure out where she went missing and save her while also figuring out about what is causing the many disappearances that have been happening on a dating app. The characters in this game are really cringy and can be hard to enjoy or even have a connection with. The story itself is alright as it does help carry the game along, but its nothing special. 
There really isn't a setting as it takes place all on a phone but its a pretty unique scenario for the player to be put in. 
The visuals are fine as it is all just meant to be a smart phone, but it does look really clean and is convincing enough to feel like a smart phone. 
Sound and audio are again fine as there is really only one bit of soundtrack when opening the game which is a pretty nice piece. The audio is a hit and miss as the audio that is used when the player makes interactions with the phone are good but the background noise that is meant to scare the player does a really poor job at that as it will get to a point where the player would have heard them enough to have no reaction towards it which is disappointing.
The gameplay is fairly simple as all you do is either select different dialog choices, do mini puzzles to load back information and finding clues to move on in the story. Gameplay is decent enough as the story that it intertwines with help it feel more satisfying to do. Finally, i do like the fact that there are multiple endings and outcomes that you experience through the game which would give it more replay-ability
Overall, Simulacra does has a few flaws but if you looking for a decent, unique experience to kill a few hours with i would definitely recommend this.

review_text_raw:
SIMULACRA scared the absolute crap out of me, and that’s one of the biggest compliments I can give a horror game. The entire game takes place through a missing person’s phone, which creates a unique and immersive experience that feels unsettlingly realistic.

What makes SIMULACRA so effective is how believable everything feels. You’re scrolling through messages, watching videos, checking social media, and uncovering clues while trying to figure out what happened. As the story progresses, things become increasingly disturbing, and there were multiple moments that genuinely made me uncomfortable in the best possible way.

The game does an excellent job building tension and mystery, making it hard to put down once you start uncovering the truth. The live-action performances help sell the story, and the feeling that something is constantly watching or manipulating events keeps you on edge throughout the entire experience.

Overall, SIMULACRA is an amazing horror game that delivers both great scares and an engaging mystery. If you’re looking for a horror experience that feels different from the usual formula, I highly recommend it.

Rating: 9/10

A genuinely creepy and immersive horror game that had me hooked from beginning to end and scared me more than I expected.

review_text_raw:
I really enjoyed this game. From the moment i started playing i was hooked on the story & what was going to happen next. 
I like hacking & decoding the messages to gain clues to help me further in the game. I am not the biggest fan of the picture puzzles however that is just my personal opinion & you do get the option to skip those as well as the messages after a few attempts.
I like there is multiple ending & I enjoyed finding out how each one impacted the story. I like how the story left you thinking of the game & its meaning.
I will say the voice acting of the characters especially greg was cringy.
The jump scares are nice and well timed out through out the game & keeps you on edge as well as the visuals in the background e.g. lights flickering. The audio is good and i enjoyed the random breathing noises etc that happened when you did certain things.
I would defo recommend this to anyone who is a horror fan & story based game fan. I am looking forward to playing the second one.

review_text_raw:
Length <3hrs

Simulacra is a Mystery game in which the player is in possession of a missing girl's phone. Using the contacts and apps on her phone you need to track down what happened to her.

Using her phone you will be looking through her life, personal messages and contracts. This will expose you to her life, how she interacted with her friends and colleagues, and what led up to her losing her phone. The transitions of the phone's main image really works well for bringing the horror into the exploration, while the missing information on her phone adds to the mystery between the events.

The puzzles were straight forward, as information I needed to access further parts of the phone easily stood out to me from when I read through her texts and messages. This helped from needing to search through every part of the phone for something I missed.

In all aspects Simulacra feels like a refinement of ‘Sara is Missing’. The texts are not as large and information felt like it was a lot simpler to find, making the game much more enjoyable to get through.

Overall I really enjoyed Simulacra, it may have what feels like weak acting and some moments of absurdity. Yet the character development is great, and looking back on her life and what led up to the moments, with the mystery behind the dating app really made the game intriguing.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z2fPdkYMW78

Looking for horrors to experience check out my curator page for more horror games worth playing: 

https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41770172/

review_text_raw:
Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.

review_text_raw:
I want to be kind to this game and for the right person, I would still recommend it. But I don't think SIMULACRA quite pulls it all off. I like the social media sleuth type games (e.g. A Normal Lost Phone.) And the horror twist on this one isn't even that bad if you don't mind breaking the whole simulationist vibe of it.

But there's quality issues. Acting and voiceover ranges from straight-faced to hammy and cartoony and it's not really clear which flavor is intended. There's also *a lot* of spelling and grammar errors that kind of break the sense of immersion. And worst of all, advancing the plot in many cases requires taking actions that the player might have a very good reason not to perform. If I suspect a character of harming the owner of this phone, why should I tell them everything I dig up from social media? Make it make sense.

[h1] A game for people with questionable morals. [/h1]

The game itself is decent, a very good idea is coupled with relatively cheap jump scares, blah blah blah.

But after finishing the game & looking through the guides for the various endings, I'm just like, "Why is the moral compass of the developers so incredibly fucked up??!"

Decide for yourselves (moderate spoilers ahead):

1. Wanna get the best ending? [spoiler]  - You have to lie to Anna's closest friend from start to finish, fool her into thinking you're Anna and even trick her into a relationship without Anna's consent. [/spoiler]

2. Wanna get an okay-ish ending? [spoiler] - You have to trust a very, VERY untrustworthy registered sex offender and send him Anna's selfies and personal emails at his request and without Anna's consent. [/spoiler]

3. Wanna get the worst ending where everyone dies? [spoiler] - You have to be an honest and decent person, protect Anna's privacy as much as possible, don't get involved with shady people and tell the truth to Anna's friends.
 [/spoiler]

Just let this sink for a moment. 
What is the game trying to teach you with this? 
I got the worst ending and the game blames me for [spoiler] not trusting Taylor. [/spoiler] How so?! My common sense says NO.
[spoiler] No, I don't feel guilty at all for not trusting a sex offender on a dating site, who would ONLY give me valuable information about RESCUING A MISSING PERSON, if I send him photos of that person without her consent in exchange. Especially since Taylor keeps making flirty jokes about this very person. He just comes across as perverted, horny and a sensationalist, and not like someone who seriously cares about Anna's well-being. Even Anna's cheating ex-boyfriend was more trustworthy than Taylor. [/spoiler]

Even in real life I would not trust such a person and would also not recommend it to anyone. The game teaches you exactly the opposite of how to behave.

开发者的想法值得肯定：通过探索陌生人的手机，来解开最终迷题。毕竟，如今，手机对我们每个人都很重要。我们都隐隐约约担心手机信息安全问题。而且，这个游戏相对来说，也并不貴。这是我推荐这个游戏的原因。
但就游戏本身而言，这个游戏比较无聊。里面的文字排序迷题，和图片迷题很无聊，对话（包括各式信息，视频中的独白等）让我昏昏欲睡。这些对话太老生常谈了，太无聊了，根本没有勾勒出有性格、让人想了解的人物形象。而对话却又恰恰是这个游戏中非常重要的一部分……

I decided to recommend it based on the innovative idea that players are required to explore a stranger's phone. It is an attractive idea, as we all care about our phones so much today. Data leaking has raised worries about data security. Plus, the price of this game is relatively low. 
However, the game is boring. The puzzles (word and pic puzzles) are humdrum, and the dialogue (messages or videos) makes me sleepy. That dialogue, which plays a crucial role in the game, has not reflected or created exciting characters—only cliche.

The best part in my opinion, is that it has a fantastic horror vibe to it without being so suspenseful that I have to take a break. I really love a horror game that gets my heart racing without making it to where I have to detach myself, and this game did that perfectly.

review_text_raw:
This game is a bit annoying. I kinda enjoyed my time with it but it's just not good.

On the plus side: it's got decent social media puzzles and a sufficiently creepy atmosphere, ... and that's about all it has going for it. On the minus side: The writing is terrible, the voice acting is not great, there are several cheap jump scares, and the story itself is awful.

Ooh, the story has multiple endings and I should play again? No thank you, once is enough. I can't see what the game could have to offer besides more weak dialogue and weird railroady decisions.

Spoilers, I guess, but I lost and got the worst ending because I didn't show enough trust in the sleazebag (who was specifically written as a sleazy dude) ALL THE WAY IN THE BEGINNING OF THE GAME. It always bunches my britches when a game does that: "Oh you didn't do a thing when you didn't have all the information yet and you couldn't make an informed decision about it? Sucks to be you, Anna's dead." Oh, and also Taylor, he's dead too. Just because I wouldn't send the sleazy dude a cute selfie of the missing girl and I wasn't sufficiently sad enough about him being caught with his pants down (literally, fuck, it's such a contrived story).

I feel like the game is less about saving Anna and more about how you're supposed to protect the feelings of the two douchebag brodudes. There's only one other recurring character, Anna's best friend, Ashley, who could have been of great help, but the story sidelines her almost immediately and only brings her back to intimate that she's secretly in love with Anna. Again, spoilers, but if you've read this far, I doubt you care. (edit: Reading someone else's review, I just learned that to get the absolute best ending, you have to catfish the best friend and reciprocate her feelings without Anna's consent or Ashley's knowledge. Cool game, bro!)

Anyway, don't bother with this game unless you really want a 5 hour puzzle game with a crappy story.

review_text_raw:
Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

review_text_raw:
SIMULACRA is a horror video game that has been highly anticipated by fans of the genre. However, after spending 1 hour playing the game, it has become clear to me that it falls far short of expectations.

One of the most disappointing aspects of SIMULACRA is the lack of polish in the graphics and sound design. The game is supposed to take place in the world of a smartphone, but the graphics are clunky and not at all realistic. The sound design is equally disappointing, with poorly implemented jump scares and music that doesn't fit the tone of the game.

The gameplay itself is also frustrating, with slow load times and confusing puzzles that are more frustrating than enjoyable. The story, which revolves around a missing person and the player's attempt to uncover the truth, is poorly executed and lacks the tension and scares that make a horror game truly effective.

In comparison to other horror games, SIMULACRA falls short in every aspect. The characters are one-dimensional and uninteresting, and the player's options for weapons and actions are limited. Even the in-game purchases feel like a desperate attempt to make up for the overall lack of quality in the game.

In my personal opinion, SIMULACRA is a major disappointment. It fails to deliver on the promise of an immersive horror experience and falls far short of the standard set by other games in the genre. I would not recommend this game to anyone and would give it a rating of 2/10.

I bought Simulacra in a bundle with the others in the series of games.

I enjoyed the experience of playing through the game, even with some dialogue choices feeling a bit unnatural.

I remain undecided on whether I'll attempt additional plays through the game for the other endings and more Steam achievements.

The story was engaging, and the characters were mostly well-played, though I thought a couple of characters with videos and audio lacked depth in their personality. The main actress did well and felt natural throughout.

I get this was probably a low-budget game as the first in the series, and I don't know what their limits were with direction and acting. But just a little bit more would have provided an unmistakable experience.

I definitely recommend playing this one, especially if you like this kind of story-driven stuff, and if it's on sale.

[code][url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/MidSeasonPro/] Mid Season Pro Group [/url] [/code]

[b]Consider following our curator page if you are satisfied with this kind of review and join our group if you want to be part of us :).[/b]


A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

review_text_raw:
Okay, so I'm a massive fan of "Sara Is Missing" which is no longer on Steam (presumably for the extreme content) which was one of the first games Kaigan Games released based on this series, I was excited to play this as I didn't realise this game was made from the same developers, I was extremely impressed! The content isn't as extreme as SIM because I think just about anyone can say that it was extremely dark and disturbing, but I think they were trialling how a game like SIM would do, and it was successful!

Enough about SIM, Simulacra is a fantastic game! The jumpscares are timed amazingly, allowing the player to calm before the next one when they least expect it. Unlike some other games when they over exaggerate the scariness. [spoiler] (I won't lie, I jumped massively at the phone reset and Taylor's jumpscare. That was cruel haha) [/spoiler] The characters are comical, [spoiler] Especially Greg with his voice notes LMFAO[/spoiler] They all have their own individual wittiness about them, personalities and not at any point did I feel like they were lack luster, they all contributed their own to the story which I really appreciate as I find a lot of horror games tend to make characters to make the player build up a connection only them to kill them in the middle or nearer towards the end.

The only critique I'd say would be the crashing, don't get me wrong! It happens to a lot of games, but I think more frequent saving should be happening or let the player save their progress manually in case it does happen. It doesn't happen often, but on the odd occasion I've needed to restart the game. Other than that, if you like a scare, thrill and a mystery; This game is for you. Plus, it's super cheap! Try it out!

review_text_raw:
SIMULACRA is a game I first saw on YouTube. I said to myself "Hey, I think I'll pick this up and give it a go. It looks good". Now, after buying it and actually playing it... I just cannot recommend it at all. It feels HEAVILY falsely advertised, to me at least due to the second trailer on steam.  Below I will state why these are my thoughts and what drove me to this conclusion.

[h1][b] My thoughts - Cons? [/b][/h1] 
⚫So to start off, the SECOND steam "TRAILER" for this game has really nothing to do with the game. You get no actual scenes like that at all. Yeah, ok... you get S O M E video scenes but it does NOT look like the second trailer in the slightest and it does not say ANYWHERE "Not actual game footage". 
⚫The game is classed as a "Horror/psychological horror" but as you play it... there is NOTHING scary about the game at all. Do not get me wrong, it had a REALLY great start to it but as you play the game gets overshadowed by "relationship issues" and it takes ALL the horror elements out of the game completely. The more in depth you go the more GOOFIER the plot actually is. Greg with his "Fu** you soooooo much" line or even the sarcastic "Sex offender" you have to talk to that CLEARLY shows who he is. Yeah... nothing mid-end of the game was good at all. 
⚫The lack-there-off accessibility options to turn down audio, adjust frames, settings in general, brightness e.t.c is non existent. You are supposed to be on a phone... come on where is the cog wheel to keep us immersed in this like a REAL phone.

[h1][b] My Verdict [/b][/h1] 
I think that there was to much HYPE based around this game due to several BIG streamers playing it (not going to mention names) and it took off as a "good horror experience" because of it. The lack of horror, accessibility options and sublime goofy plot makes this a dull, boring experience that will leave you feeling like this -  "What did I just spend my time playing" "Was it worth it" "Can I get a refund". 

[h1][b] 3/10 - A goofy plot leads to bad horror experience. [/b][/h1]

Full playthrough took me about 6 hours and it was amazing – the gameplay is very simple, you just go through the found smartphone, but it is so fresh and original that you can’t stop diving deeper into the gameplay and story; the story itself is very catchy and it mediates between a cool (and I mean really cool) horror story and kind of detective, where you need to solve smart, interesting puzzles. But here are the important things: it does not feel like just a solving puzzles, you literally investigating a very strange and creepy case, everything feels so alive and real (characters, surfing through the mail, chatting, etc.) and most important that it creates a strong feeling that the choices matter – crazy plot twists, extreme tension, and the sense of realism; about horror –  it’s just perfect, not very much of it but it is placed at the right moments and always hits at the right time. 
It definitely gives me some cool vibes that are crazy mix between “laptop” horror movies (Open Windows, Unfriend) and oldschool “teenager” horrors series (Tales From The Crypt, Are You Afraid Of The Dark?). One of the best games I’ve played for a long time and definitely a hidden gem. 
Do I recommend this game? Strongly recommend.

review_text_raw:
Love this game. In the same vein as films like 'Searching', you spend all of your time navigating a device (in this case a phone) in search of a missing person. Simulacra has more a horror tone than 'Searching', but for much of the game's runtime it's only lightly scary, with most of the suspense coming not from supernatural frights but from further unraveling the mystery by feeling like an amateur cybersleuth. 

There are definitely moments where it was frustrating trying to figure out where to go next, but the game generally does a good job of pointing you in the right direction through the use of hints given by the characters in the game. It all feels organic and never too forced. Multiple playthroughs will be needed to see all of the endings, but even just one playthrough will give every player a satisfying experience in the end. 

My few gripes with this game are that the actors aren't really that great in their performances, and for a game that I think is set in the US (at least that seems like the accent everyone is going for), the actor's accents waver quite often. This is obviously not a big budget production, so it's understandable that top shelf talent isn't within reach, but I would say that instead of trying to force a setting, just go with what's available around you. I don't feel that the US setting is necessary to tell this kind of story. I'd also like if there were some way to expedite replays of the game. Yes, if you do a second playthrough you can skip text much more quickly, but I'm thinking of something kinda like Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. In that title there was a branching path menu you could pull up and jump exactly to the point where the story diverged. That would save so much time replaying up until the point where a critical decision was made. 

Conclusion:

Fun cyberdetective game told through a smartphone. Elements of horror, but nothing too overdone so that non-horror fans couldn't enjoy. Gameplay makes you do a fair amount of thinking, without too much handholding, so you feel a sense of accomplishment when you unearth another clue. Tons of easter eggs are there for those willing to look. Performances are not great here, but the voiced parts are minimal and don't interrupt the flow too often. 

Playtime: 4.4 hrs
100% completion

review_text_raw:
Picture this: you find a girl's phone, and her name is Anna. But here's the catch - she's missing, and you're the one holding her phone with all its personal information. Creepy, right?

The story revolves around investigating Anna's disappearance, and as you interact with her friends and family through text messages and phone conversations, the tension keeps building up. The drama feels real, and the game's decision-based mechanics force you to make choices that affect the outcome. The best part is, it's not just a mystery unraveling over time; your main goal is clear - find Anna. But beware, Simulacra is not just about jumpscares; it plays with your senses more subtly, with eerie audio effects that might even make you question reality outside the game.

Though the game is quite engaging, it's not without its flaws. The voice acting feels a bit awkward and scripted, and some audio elements seem unnecessary, primarily existing for the sake of providing a jumpscare. But hey, the recorded videos are well done, especially Anna's personal vlogs.

Playing this game on PC might not be as immersive as on a mobile phone but it holds its merit reguardless. Still, they could've allowed portrait mode like in Downwell to make it even better.

All in all, Simulacra is a decent horror title that excels in subtle horror and decision-based gameplay. It really makes you think about privacy, honesty, and data security, and that's something you don't often get from a horror game. So, if you're up for an unnerving experience that's a bit different from the usual horror games, give Simulacra a try!

Simulacra is a found phone horror game with cutscenes that is only fun once. I really wish I could give this a medium review as it is not entirely bad...


Aesthetics:
I gotta say the aesthetics are  a bit dated. It pretty much screams early 2010 but the horror aspect is still pretty good! The acting in the cutscenes is okay but not the best.

Story:
Premise of a haunted found phone is pretty cool. The story is alright but the characters are getting super annoying pretty fast and are just not that believable to be honest. The puzzles are okay but the game really, really drags on and on. Yes, there are multiple endings but when you are done with one ending you don't really feel like seeing the others...
Also the good endings are achieved by not being a decent human being?
The horror aspect gets lost due its sideplots and the climax was actually ... not scary but just weird?

Gameplay:
Puzzle solving. You try to retrive data from her phone and really invade her privacy to be honest. At first it is interesting but I felt pretty bad trying to go really personal stuff of hers.

review_text_raw:
There is a first time for everything, it seems. In this case, it is digging through someone's phone to find out more about her life, connections, steps and what happened to her. Never have I ever done this before.
Anna is the missing woman's name and we get our hands on her phone. As an outsider, we are supposed to find her by solving nice puzzles. The outcome of this game seems to be heavily dependent on the choices the player makes, which are mostly the answers to dialogues and steps one takes. Even in the first playthrough, I did not need any guide to solve the puzzles, which is nice. Some were challenging enough to delay the end of the game a little bit. Multiple endings give you the possibility to replay the game and see, what different answers and a different playstyle will lead to.
Had some resolution issue on Win11home64 and Nvidia GPU, but playing it in windowed mode (by hitting alt+enter) worked perfectly fine and did not "ruin" the flair of the game. Great dialogues and voice actors! A lot of love was put in this game, it seems. Well done, Kaigan Games! Terima kasih!

review_text_raw:
This is a very acclaimed horror game for its unique format, solving a mystery remotely through a victim's cell phone. And for that I was very interested! And those elements I was looking for, it delivered.

I do have other issues, though. While I feel like this is creepy and atmospheric set-up that would lend itself well to horror scenarios like a serial killer or modern hauntings, I wasn't as grabbed by the big bad revealed in the climax [spoiler]what with the more SciFi twist with commentary on a modern person's internet persona vs their true selves, especially since there seemed to be at least some vague supernatural ability given to this system that is never expanded upon[/spoiler]. Though, with the very apparent and similar themes to this series' free-to-play title [i]Simulacra: Pipe Dreams[/i] which I have completed previously, I'm not sure what else I expected.

These games are cheap enough, with gimmicky-enough gameplay and good enough atmosphere that doesn't overstay its welcome with a pretty short playtime that I overall still really like it. The way the live action footage is used to weave a narrative was iconic for the time, after all, to where upon release I saw people playing this everywhere. I'd say I'm just happy enough to say that not only did I enjoy this game but I'm interested in what became of the next couple of games.

But note: I also couldn't get this game working for the longest time - I bought it forever ago and just got it to work on the day I'm writing this. It was missing some kind of runtime package that another game's install eventually provided. So keep that in mind. That was a pain.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a horror graphic / text adventure (I don't know how else I could define it). 

Story and Characters, two main characteristics of the genre, are really weak. What bothered me the most, though, was the interface and the gameplay. Players only use during the whole game Anna's smartphone and mess with her social media accounts, messages and so on, in order to find out what happened to her. I feel like we already spend way too much time using these technologies and social media, so I didn't enjoy this experience so much.

You may find this concept interesting, though. In this case the game is worth the price, since there are several endings and Easter Eggs to be discovered in multiple runs (I got only a couple of them, though).

It really depends on how much you share my opinion, whether you should buy this game or not. If you feel that the mentioned aspects may annoy you, you'd better use your money and time in other games. Otherwise you can give Simulacra a try.

Now that I've 100% this one - Simulacra is good, but Simulacra 2 is definitely an improvement. The premise is intriguing, the gameplay is intuitive, and the fact there are multiple endings is satisfying (and the non-diegetic-seeming sounds definitely fooled me a few times, as if they were truly happening). Need for more proofreading aside. it's solid and fun.

review_text_raw:
It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

review_text_raw:
A fantastic exercise in intrigue, suspense, horror, social commentary, with well-considered player choice and interactivity. There are a great many wonderful touches to truly immerse you in using a missing person's phone. It's completely diegetic and naturalistic, never straying from the phone's interface. And if you're interested in the idea of desperately looking through someone's phone to find any trace of them, going down a deeper and deeper rabbit hole, you absolutely need to play this game. It is unmatched by any of its peers.

Just keep in mind the production value, so if you're expecting AAA industry level acting from this modest indie studio, remember this is a game made by a small team where you're on a typical phone of an ordinary woman with unremarkable colleagues. Its brilliance lies in the presentation, concept, and suspense. The production flaws and minor mechanical limitations are quick to forgive, and going through again on Begin+ easily makes up for it in my opinion.

review_text_raw:
I'm going to divide this review into various sections based on gameplay elements, in a slightly illogical order. This seems appropriate for a slightly illogical game. Also, I ran out of characters, so I had to leave a lot out.

[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Best part of the game. Only thing that makes it scary.

Even for someone who had quite a few scares spoiled for me due to watching previous playthrough snippits and common internet knowledge, the scares still all GOT ME. And, I mean, they GOT ME. I was jumping in my seat and looking around for the voices I was hearing. At one point [spoiler] I heard a door knocking and thought someone was trying to break into my bedroom [/spoiler]. Those sounds that play, whether phone ringing or human breathing or that terrible [spoiler] wood knocking [/spoiler], were still enough to make me jump after four straight playthroughs. Every time, I'd finish, and I'd think, this is no Doki Doki Literature Club, I can get through this without jumping. But then there'd be a cellphone ringing or glitched sound or Anna breathing at me and, however slight, I'd jump. The sound in this game was so effective it almost wasn't fair. 

That said, the only thing that was what I can only accurately describe as mid was the voice for the [spoiler] Simulacra [/spoiler]. I'll go into this later, but I got to the end of the game so freaked out by the sound at the beginning, that this didn't leave much an impact.

[h2] Music [/h2]
There isn't as much to gush about here. I'd say it does its job and the title screen is iconic.Part of me wishes I had some more songs to add to my gamer Main Character Syndrome Spotify playlist, but I also do think limiting the soundtrack and sticking to eiry silence cut off by that terrifying sound design is the way to go.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
If I ever found a missing person's phone, and everyone treated me like this, I'd either 1. Say she's better off missing or 2. Just hand the phone off to the cops. 

[h3] Anna [/h3]
They really try to make her sympathetic. She's rejected from vet school and she's just gotten out of a toxic relationship, her workplace is awful and she's being harrassed by her boss and coworker. Now, with all that laid out, you might be wondering, what don't you like about her? She's clearly very layered and passionate and look at all the bad stuff happening to her. She's so sympathetic!

Yes, there are lots of bad things happening to her. But other than the fact that she likes animals and is really bad at picking people to be around, I can't tell you one thing about her. She's just very bland. Honestly, I wonder if it would be more interesting if it was Greg we were supposed to find. Be told by everyone how important it is to hunt him down and bring him back, slowly uncovering that he's not that great of a person, having to contemplate with the consequences of what it would mean to actually bring the jerk back. Anna being the one we need to bring back is just kind of...eh? These people really want her back in their lives and whole time I was just wondering, why? She's cardboard. 

[h3] Taylor [/h3]
He tells bad jokes but you can tell deep down he's got a big heart. He's made some big mistakes and honestly comes off as a bit of a creep. I wasn't sure what exactly he liked about Anna, but that's beside the point. Actually, yeah, that is my only gripe with him. Why is he so invested in the life of a chick he's talked to on a dating app one time? I mean this man goes to her and begs for her and puts himself in danger for her. That's a lot of work for cardboard you saw on sale on Ebay. 

[h3] Greg [/h3]
People like to rip on the actor for this guy, and yeah, I get it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to be laughing at him or if he was supposed to tick me off or if heaven forbid he was supposed to scare me, but he did two of three (i'm sure you can guess which ones). I think Greg sees Anna as someone who he can easily control and manipulate. Which makes sense. She is cardboard. I did find it odd on one route where he [spoiler] suddenly abandons pursuing Anna as soon as he learns the cops are after him [/spoiler]. It came out of left field and then you never learn what happens to him from that point. Honestly, I love to hate Greg, so I think he does his job. I can understand him being obsessive over Anna since 1. they dated for two years and 2. she sees her as easy. 

[h3] Ashley [/h3]
THIS GIRL TICKED ME OFF. I'm not talking about the route where you [spoiler] lie to her and manipulate her into saying she's in love with Anna, though again I ask WHY [/spoiler]. I'm talking about how she treats you if you come clean right away and just tell her who you are and why you have Anna's phone. She flips, gets super defensive. won't let you explain yourself, and then calls the cops on you. She'll randomly disappear from the plot and go offline, and she won't work with you no matter what you say to her. I find that highly improbable. I don't think they knew what to do with Ashley for the routes where [spoiler] she knows the truth [/spoiler].

[h3] Everyone else [/h3]
Nothing much to report. No one made me as mad as Anna's supposed BFF. So good job.

[h3] Simulacra [/h3]
Alright, I have an issue. This thing isn't scary. There's so much buildup, then it's just kind of there. It's so melodramatic and easy to make fun of. I almost think this story would've been better of Greg had just killed her or something. I don't understand how this thing kills or kidnaps, I'm not scared of it, and it keeps changing the rules. I dunno, I just wanted one last big scare, or something that felt satisfying after all that buildup. Then I saw it, and I thought, that's it?

[h2] Story [/h2]
In this game you find a phone that is clearly possessed, and are tasked to find its owner, Anna. You are helped and hindered by the various people trying to get ahold of her, and you can either leave her life in shambles for her to return to or make her life better with your interference.

It's a cool concept and I enjoyed most of it, but at the end it all just falls apart horribly.

The antagonist is just a goofy "social media bad" message that isn't explained in even the slightest. All the "good" endings come from being an atrocious human being who constantly lies, violates privacy flagrantly, implicitly trusts a sex offender and an abuser with intimate details, deceives the police, etc. If you were to play this as if you were actually trying to solve a potential kidnapping / murder, you're 100% getting the worst possible ending and have to start over from scratch.

This is "ignore red flags and trust all men", the game. It's downright crazy that a supernatural horror game about a missing woman fails the Bechdel test.

review_text_raw:
A fun, innovative experience involving navigating someone’s digital life to find out what happened to someone.

Background: I like playing interactive stories like this while I’m eating instead of watching TV or a movie. It’s good to play these kinds of games between bites.

I didn’t know what to make of this game—I think I got it as part of a bundle—but installed it and tried it out after running through a few movie games and wanting to shift to something else. I was pleasantly surprised by the story, and the gameplay was similar to games like Her Story and Orwell where you interact with a digital interface to make the story unfold.

The Positives:
-It really does feel like you are a person who found a phone and are trying to find out what happened to the owner. There are a few times where it is imperfect in terms of what you probably could/should/would do, but it does a good enough job that it felt realistic enough to suspend disbelief for several hours.

-The phone was fun to play around with—you go into various apps and learn about the owner’s recent activity and then even get to participate a little.

-The people you interact with are sketchy as hell, but it definitely made things interesting.

-The ending got pretty wild; while the horror elements are minimal for most of the game, the ending combines the genres of tech-thrillers and evil-spirit-horror—very interesting. It’s not simply like System Shock 2 or Terminator (where the tech tries to control you) or Evil Dead or The Ring (where evil spirits are trying to kill you); it’s an interesting mix.

-The people involved did a great job—there are a lot of photos, videos, and conversations, and both the actors and the developers did a great job of making it all fit together. It all felt real—I never thought for a moment that the photos or videos were “fake” or “made-for-the-game”. That’s all I look for in acting; not everything has to be Meryl Streep, and this felt real enough.

-The ending was fresh for me—the combination of it being just slightly different from other endings in the genre along with the uniqueness of me having to make decisions that led to the outcome made the experience very new and interesting.

The Negatives:
-As I mentioned, the people you interact with are sketchy, which I overall enjoyed but it does result in some weird interactions. I thought it worked, but I wouldn’t be surprised if you played and said, “Why don’t they just do X?” — I felt that any plot holes were covered up well enough for me to buy it, but you might not.

-If you like a lot of horror, there isn’t much here—it ratchets up near the end but for the most part is more of a mystery with a dash of spooky/thriller elements. I liked the amount, but you might want more.

-It’s tough to strike a balance between elements that build the character and world with ones that begin to give you hints about the mystery…I think they did a good job, but you might find that early on you go through a lot of videos and photos that don’t reveal much. The photos are easy enough to skim through, but you’ll watch several videos and they don’t really do much other than give you a live look at what the owner looked like while slowly introducing the fact that something is amiss. If you’re a narrative critic, you’d probably want them to have done more with those elements than just a look into the life of the owner.

Overall, it’s an interesting game. I was engaged most of the time and there are only brief periods where there is a lot of text back-and-forth that you might want something more to be happening—but it’s not bad by any means. If you are sucked in at those points, you will enjoy it. If not, that’s probably where you might tune out. The good news is that the developers listened and put in the ability to adjust the speed, etc. of the game (especially if you’re replaying it) to solve for that issue. So I think you’ll be okay. As long as you like the mysterious look-into-the-life-of-someone-else genre of point-and-click games (like the “found footage” genre of movies but for video games), you’ll enjoy it. If you are hoping for a lot of horror, though, there isn’t too much and so I just hope to set your expectations appropriately.

review_text_raw:
I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

review_text_raw: I've played a few found phone games. This one has some of the most realistic "puzzles", like finding out someone's last name by looking up their contact info, or a birthday through a photo's date taken. The game also gives you hints when you are stuck, and the UI also feels realistic (complete with losing your progress in one app while going to check in another sometimes). However, the writing was not good. I can understand some typos when people are texting, but the copy on websites should be a step up. I didn't like how you had to [spoiler]work with three guys who were crappy to Anna in different ways, and then keep your identity hidden from her best[/spoiler] in order to advance the game or get the best ending. What would you do if a stranger left their phone at your doorstep? Would you try to unlock it and snoop around? Of course you would! And this is the story of Simulacra.

This is a strait forward puzzle game where one has to dig through a stranger’s phone, and talk to third parties through their device, to unlock the mystery of their disappearance. Over all this isn’t a hard game to figure out and a single play through can be competed in a couple hours with minimal effort. 

Additional play throughs are sped up with a “Begin +” mode; Which makes messages appear faster but there are a ton of unskippable moments that make achievement hunting a chore. That second, and third, play through was rough… 

Worth  a couple bucks for a single play through, but, regardless of ending, it’s painful to get through multiple times. If there was a way to skip the redundancy, this would have been a perfect achievement hunters’ game.

- Intriguing

review_text_raw:
Little FMV interactive story telling game from Asian Devs, where you have to play like a Stalker / Hacker who finds a stranger's phone and has to find out what happened to the original owner.
Probably brings about 2-3 hours of semi-original fun for the main story line and one ending (of four), well worth it for the cheap price (if it's on sale) - I for instance bought Simulacra 1+2 for only 1.2€ and am already happy getting my money's worth after playing only the first part, gonna play the second one too, but beware the most expensive and newest third part is supposedly crappy according to reviews, so not gonna bother with that one.

A few Pros and Cons:

Pros:
+ neat little game, cheap price, semi-original story and idea

+ multiple Endings, somewhat of replayability (though not much)

+ some interesting charachters, an unknown protagonist, possible similarities to real live 
   dating crimes (educational)

+ some interesting Achievements in and outside of the main story line

+ nice positive review link @ the end if you liked the game & none if you click on didn't like it^^

+ very good price (at least while on sale or from external site) for Part 1&2 (not 3 though)

Cons:
- there are some small Bugs, like Soundclip getting stuck repeating in endless loop,
  or starting a vlog video while simultaneously getting a call freezes screen sideways so it gets 
  stuck and you have to restart from last checkpoint

- quite a few (very) missable Achievements, have to play at least 4 times to get them all
  (though with continue/new game+ text speed is much faster, so won't take that long)

- not many options / settings, like missing mute sound etc.

- sometimes the English wording is off (missing words, wrong grammar, etc.),
  not sure if due to Asian Dev or simulating the real chatting experience

- quite linear, except for the 4 different endings and a few choices, choices in general don't matter much,
  mostly you get like 3 Dialog options for chats etc., but in most cases it will all result in the same, maybe one 
  added sentence or a word or two changed and stuff like that


All in all I do recommend it to anyone who likes FMV / interactive and/or invesitgative / mystery Genre games.

P.S. Ashley is hot, sorry I sound like the Taylor Perv now, who is also a interesting charachter <3

review_text_raw: This game had a slate of good ideas executed poorly. There are a ton of grammar mistakes in the English version that make situations unclear, and make the actions of characters within the story seem unrealistic, or come out of nowhere. The writing seems to come from a very immature perspective that seems to commodify women as sex objects. A lot of the game seems to want you to comply with the demands of the male characters, while the sole female character that knew the victim is uncooperative and aggressive toward you. The game chastised me for failing to get a guy to trust me, because he lied about having information I needed and wanted me to send him a picture of the victim from her phone in exchange for said information he didn't have. And even though I told him that was creepy and he seemed to understand, he later blew up at me for it and got himself killed. There's no sense of accountability, consistency, or predictability in these incredibly unrealistic interactions, and if it weren't for the lacking in that area of writing (and the sometimes horrible voice acting -- I'm looking at you, Greg), this could have actually been a very compelling and immersive game. Instead, the lack of payoff and random interactions render it a complete waste of time.

review_text_raw:
Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.
