review_text_raw:
So... this is one of those game I already watched someone (Jacksepticeye) play it, but 7 years is a long time and I forgot the fun little details.

Cons
-Oml, Greg and Cassie's voice actors... that was rough listening to. Taylor's cringe shower serenade tipped into a con for me.
-Some of the word puzzles were a bit tricky
--Just having picture and word puzzles is a bit weird for a horror game like this... but without it, it isn't really a game, I guess.
-Someone needs to check on Ashley, she is always drunk texting Anna...
-Anna is wearing the same thing in each of her vlogs... lol.
--Speaking of, boom mic appearance in one of those vlogs, and a man that isn't one of the actors as well in the vlogs.
-I'm fine with all the horror ambiance... but seriously... knocking?! I could understand for one certain scene, but those knocking cues makes me pause the game and make sure no one is knocking like a maniac on my office. The subtle knocks are worse than the banging knocking.
-Ofc one of the photos is Anna in a towel, lol.
-The most unbelievable thing? Even in 2017, a phone with only 6 apps, 3 of which are e-mail, text, and phone, is completely mystifying, lol. The other three are Internet, Tinder, and Twitter.
-One bad interaction with a certain character, and there goes three of the four endings. Bummer.

Pros
-I mean... it is an award-winning story. It went off of Black Mirror's coat tails, but who cares?
-Apart from the lack of apps... the phone looks lived in. It's a crappy phone that you have to do puzzles to read texts that are sent to you, so there's that, lol.
--The pictures that are just in there to give atmosphere truly did the job... namely because it isn't just Anna in the same outfit like the vlogs, lol. Actually made me like Greg for a second...
-The horror is ear-screeching and visual and audio jumpscares... so... not terrible.
-Right length of game, roughly 3 to 3 and a half hours.
-Pretty nice detective game
-Aside from Taylor's serenade, him, Anna, and Ashley's actors contributed nicely to the story

Honestly, its the length that is making me recommend it the most. Short story, in and out, and it makes running for the other endings less of a trudge.

I could understand for one certain scene, but those knocking cues makes me pause the game and make sure no one is knocking like a maniac on my office. The subtle knocks are worse than the banging knocking. -Ofc one of the photos is Anna in a towel, lol. -The most unbelievable thing? Even in 2017, a phone with only 6 apps, 3 of which are e-mail, text, and phone, is completely mystifying, lol. The other three are Internet, Tinder, and Twitter. -One bad interaction with a certain character, and there goes three of the four endings. Bummer. Pros -I mean... it is an award-winning story. It went off of Black Mirror's coat tails, but who cares? -Apart from the lack of apps... the phone looks lived in. It's a crappy phone that you have to do puzzles to read texts that are sent to you, so there's that, lol. --The pictures that are just in there to give atmosphere truly did the job... namely because it isn't just Anna in the same outfit like the vlogs, lol. Actually made me like Greg for a second... -The horror is ear-screeching and visual and audio jumpscares... so... not terrible. -Right length of game, roughly 3 to 3 and a half hours. -Pretty nice detective game -Aside from Taylor's serenade, him, Anna, and Ashley's actors contributed nicely to the story Honestly, its the length that is making me recommend it the most. Short story, in and out, and it makes running for the other endings less of a trudge.

review_text_raw:
[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

review_text_raw:
Fun game for something quite different, a bit like a detective style game using a phone interface to get to the truth.

GOOD STUFF: To me, i enjoyed it for the novelty, and there are different endings for your choices.... They have tried some unique puzzle ideas, you do have to go back and forth through lots of phone based media to solve stuff, and the game often gives you options for hints, if you want them, when stuck instead of just straight delivering them to you after 2 seconds.  They tried to capture how the current world of social media and dating can feel and added some light humour throughout the game.  if you like solving crime style puzzles with a little mystery element added on top, it is worth the short playtime for a bit of fun.

BAD STUFF: However the ridiculous immaturity/selfishness/general mood of ALL the characters had me struggling to want to side with, save or even continue to want to interact with almost any of them as the game went on... It almost makes sense, as they are around 20yrs of age, that they would be a little naive, hot headed, horny and impulsive but yeesh.... waaaaay overboard, none of them ever understand if you do anything for the safety of yourself OR them, and so much of the dialogue has an extreme teen gossip feel, omg he said that you said that she did THAAAAT guurrrrrl im not talking for 2 mins to show I hate you!!! :O haha!  
Similarly the options you can choose between often force you to move the game onwards in a way I would never even consider and would actively steer clear of if I was in this situation.... but I understand it's very difficult to set up enough paths for players to feel like they really have a choice with these things.... Still some work could be done to not feeeeeel like your responses are so forced in a certain direction.  Maybe I missed it too at the start? But suggesting your character is unable to speak or something would help make some of the game moments easier to understand/improve immersion as well.

I really appreciate what the devs have done here, and hope they continue to make some fun games with a difference to the standard algorithm stuff that floods the markets these days. It would be great if they can find a way to let characters adapt to understand the players personality and choices a little more, it's so important to games like this where you are expected to solve a crisis situation if it feels even remotely like it was your actual choices as a person that led to the consequences you get :).

**Simulacra: A Creepy, Addictive Mystery (But Please, Give Me a Volume Setting)**

I hecking love the story in Simulacra. It’s immersive, unsettling, and keeps me hooked. So far, I’ve only completed one ending, but I’ll definitely dive back in when I feel like emotionally wrecking myself again.

That said, why is there no in-game volume setting? I had to manually adjust my mixer volume in Windows just to avoid jumpscares destroying my ears. It’s a small thing, but it makes a huge difference—please, devs, let me control my suffering levels properly. I also have problem on not seeing my own cursor in the game too

Despite that, I’m loving the experience so far, and I can’t wait to see what other endings have in store for me (or how badly I’ll mess things up next time). If you love eerie, found-footage style mysteries, this game is definitely worth playing!

review_text_raw:
[b]Simulacra[/b] is a "found phone" game—a genre where players uncover clues after discovering a stranger's lost smartphone. While the concept has gained popularity in the last decade, games have experimented with faux interfaces mimicking imagined technology for years. I remember playing Mean Streets and the officially licensed X-Files game, both of which attempted something similar.

In Simulacra, you navigate the protagonist's phone within the game's tightly controlled framework, piecing together what happened to its owner. I was initially drawn to the game due to the resurgence of modern full-motion video (FMV) storytelling. Having enjoyed 2015's Her Story, I expected a similar experience. While Simulacra integrates FMV clips effectively, its "found phone" premise was far less compelling to me. I think I hit an audience mismatch—I’m simply not a fan of smartphones. Since I don't particularly enjoy using my own phone, the idea of rifling through someone else’s was unappealing. I played on my laptop and embarrassingly took about a third of the game to realize that it was undoubtedly designed to be played on a smartphone—duh.

The protagonist, Anna, feels like a generic twenty-something woman struggling with rocky relationships, an unfulfilling job, and repeated rejections in her academic and professional pursuits. [spoiler]She has a non-binary best friend, which the game seemingly frames as a revelation, but it’s so heavily telegraphed that it falls into cliché territory.[/spoiler] In fact, Anna herself is a walking cliché, as is the familiar "technology is evil" theme—an overused trope in uninspired sci-fi narratives. After seeing it so often, it no longer has much impact for me.

The game’s title did surprise me. Before playing, I had never encountered the terms "Simulacra" or "Simulacrum," which piqued my curiosity. Midway through, I looked up the meaning, wondering why a game about a woman's lost phone would have such a name. Ah, crap—spoilers.

As for gameplay, Simulacra offers little freedom. Players must follow rigidly scripted conversations in a precise order to unlock new options and clues. While there are minor choices in how you interact with Anna’s close friends, they ultimately boil down to a few dialogue changes that determine which of the five endings you get—most of which depend on choices made in the last 10% of the game. That said, I appreciated that I could make all the necessary connections without resorting to a guide or hints. That sense of progress and accomplishment is something lacking in other puzzle or adventure games.

Overall, Simulacra is predictable but not necessarily bad. The FMV clips are well-integrated, Wendy Van Horen Carneiro delivers a solid performance as the wronged damsel in distress, and the faux-phone interface is thoughtfully designed. I give it a [b]3 out of 5[/b]—though the game is clearly aimed at a different audience than me, so others may find it more engaging.

i really enjoyed the game. managed to not find out anything about the game in advance, so i went in knowing absolutely nothing.
somehow it dawned on me incredibly late, that my actions actually have consequences.
there were clear hints to it, but i somehow only saw it as a little thing that doesn't actually affect the ending, so i was very positively surprised to see there were different endings.
the characters and their motives and personalities were all very engaging and i truly liked finding out more about them. there's also replayability for finding the other endings, which is a very nice feature.

on an unrelated but very important note: this game gets a 0 out of 10 in terms of motion sickness.
absolutely no motion sickness for me and thus perfectly playable. i appreciate some good horror games that do not make me suffer on physical levels.

review_text_raw:
I liked the concept and the general gameplay, but I was disappointed with the ending, especially after finishing my first playthrough and following a guide so I can see the "perfect" ending this time around. In general the game felt a bit too "handholdy" and forced you go through certain conversations or actions before you could progress with the plot despite figuring out what to do next. A few plot points made a little to no sense + at least I never found out why and how you obtained the phone. Overall I'm happy with the game, especially considering that I paid only 0.79€ for it on sale. 

[spoiler]Having to manipulate Ashley and being way too open with Taylor who can be a bit creepy at times and who could have easily been the one behind the disappearance felt wrong yet somehow it's supposedly the right thing to do. I also felt like the story assumes you to be a guy based on some of the dialogue which slightly decreased the immersion for me considering you're basically a faceless and voiceless protagonist and can easily insert yourself into the story for most of the game. Unrelated, but I hope Anna feels the same way about Ashley, at least Anna's Spark had both men and women available for swiping so I suppose there is a chance? #bivisibility [/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
I picked up this game for less than a pack of gums, and it's phenomenal for the price you pay for it. It reminded me of [i] Her Story, [/i] another indie game that was released 2 years before this, so if you liked that, you'll like this as well. It is also similar to [i] Life is Strange, Until Dawn, the Telltale games, Deus Ex Human Revolution, [/i] but this is much lighter and made by a smaller team. 

Unlike the games mentioned earlier, your choices actually matter. If you go in thinking "oh I'm going to play this game and I'll get the good ending and I'll be done with it", then you're wrong. It doesn't work like that, and you can screw up your ending very early on. If [i] Until Dawn [/i] let you save the characters you want by using common sense, Simulacra is not as forgiving. Even if you try to reason with the characters like in [i] Deus Ex, [/i] that's not always going to work. The overall story is entertaining and the characters are great, however, there are some typos, the voice calls are cheesy because they're overdone, being shot in a studio, and the game tries to scare you with its ambience sounds, which aren't connected to the story in any way. There are also some puzzles, some easier, others are harder, which make the game more enjoyable as it's not that linear and actually puts up a challenge.

Overall, I found the game enjoyable. It's replayable, the choices that you make actually have some sort of impact, and the characters are great. There's also a Simulacra spin-off that is free, and there are some sequels. If you didn't get the ending that you wished for, don't feel bad. Some endings are easier to get than others.

The theme music is an absolute banger, though.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10

Game looks and interacts well enough, but inconsistent writing and deeply unlikable characters detract from the experience. Narrow limits on how you can interact with the phone as well as how you can respond to the various characters (your dialogue choices), coupled with an extremely detached feeling from choices to their consequences left me feeling deeply disappointed by the end. 

And I'm absolutely NOT about to replay it (at least) 3 more times, following HIGHLY SPECIFIC requirements across 4hr-long runthroughs to see what else is there ending-wise.

Not recommended, unfortunately.

review_text_raw:
You've obtained the phone of a missing woman named Anna. Your goal is to snoop around her phone's files, social media, and her contacts to get more information about who may have taken her. 

The game simulates what it's like to be in this situation very well with the phone and notification sounds. It feels both dangerous and scandalous at the same time. Like at any moment, police will be knocking on your door asking why you have her phone. 

I actually got a bit invested in figuring out what was going on, but I also wanted to be a terrible person and mislead people to see what would happen. 

Who are you relative to the situation? 
Maybe you're the one who kidnapped her! 
Play the game to see for yourself because I do recommend it.

The main thing dragging back the game isn't the story. It's not the immoral conversations you are having with Anna's abusive ex boyfriend, Greg. It's not even about the advice you're taking from register sex offender, Taylor. 

It's just the cringe acting. 

Honestly that's it. 

The acting is awful, like really acting. Anna sounds like she's reading from a script. Same applies to all characters. From Taylor's singing to Greg cursing you out, these people cannot act.

Another issue is investment in the characters, I don't like any of them so I don't feel for any of them. 

Also the characters are stupid, simply stupid. None of them decide to ever call you out for being a potential suspect, and only one calls the cops after a while.

I'm not a fan of horror genre. I find stupid main characters hard to root for, and just like horror movies on Netflix, I've lowered my expectations to just enjoy the slop.

It's a well put together game, with a believable UI for a Samsung phone.

review_text_raw:
A nice surprise. The idea is great, you found a phone and need to find out what happened to its owner by going through her internet history, emails, texts, onlinde dating app, etc.

The performances of the cast are uneven, with the main character thankfully doing a good job, but some others sounding really unnatural. This is more of a detective game than a puzzle game, and I think they could actually have done without the little "put the words in the right order and reconstruct the image" things and just focus only on the story but that's fine.
It does feel like we're stepping into someone's private life, and it does feel a little bit creepy doing so but that's the point, even though some interaction seem forced ([spoiler]who does a job interview by texts for instance[/spoiler]) but you have to suspend your disbelief in order to appreciate this original detective story (the end is a little bit disappointing but not as much as ruining the whole story for me).

review_text_raw:
Great take on found footage horror. There's not a lot of "game" to be played here, as much as it is an interactive story, however it's well written and easy to get drawn into.

Basically, you find a phone, discover the owner is missing, and things get very weird while trying to track them down. The story is a bit heavily railroaded, but there are multiple endings and the responses you choose while playing affect your outcome. 
 
A few good jump scares, eerie narrative, and satisfying to investigate. The acting leaves room for improvement, but it is what it is.

As a huge fan of the found footage genre, I absolutely recommend giving this one a chance.

review_text_raw:
Unsettling. Unseen horrors. You feel as though you truly found someone's phone and have to uncover all their dark secrets to find out what happened. 

Simulacra is an amazing little rabbit hole of a game; a found‑phone thriller that feels intimate, invasive, and surprisingly reactive. Even though my first playthrough ended in the bad ending, with both Taylor and Anna dying, it didn’t sour the experience at all. If anything, it made me realize just how many branching paths and character‑shaping choices I’d only brushed past.

What stands out most is how much influence you actually have over the people you’re texting. The tone you take, the pressure you apply, the empathy you show (or don’t); it all ripples outward in ways that feel organic rather than scripted. That makes every conversation feel like a little puzzle of its own, and it’s easy to get pulled into the illusion that you’re really trying to save someone on the other end of the screen.

There’s also a surprising amount of content tucked into the phone that I completely missed on my first run. I was so worried about the battery dying that I missed returning to the emails and missed the final vlog. That tension is part of the charm, though;  the sense that you’re racing against something truly evil on the other side of the screen.

The result is a game with genuine replayability. Multiple endings, branching character arcs, and hidden threads make it worth diving back in, especially once you know the stakes and can explore the phone more confidently.
If you like narrative mysteries with a voyeuristic twist and choices that actually matter, Simulacra is absolutely worth your time;  even if your first ending is a tragic one.

review_text_raw:
I watched a playthrough of this game back in 2018, and I remember really liking it back then! When I was reminded of it's existence and heard positive buzz around it, I decided to try my hand at it. It is rather dated in some ways - the inclusion of a Twitter parody app, for one, and even the way characters post on that app scream early 2010's, and the other ways it's aged are just simply Millenialcore humor throughout - it also has quite a few typos (some more distracting than others), some of the voice acting is rough ("fuuuuuck thiiis sooooo muuuuuch" is now a repeated reference in my friend group for the absolutely baffling delivery lol). The plot and gimmicks are also rather predictable if you're at all familiar with this sub genre of horror media and akin sub genres. I recall the plot beats and phone gimmick/framing device being somewhat novel back in 2018, but maybe I misremember.

All that being said, I do enjoy this game and I think it's still worth playing! Some of my favorite things about this game are the soundscape (particularly the knocking and breathing noises randomly interspersed throughout), the interactivity and surprisingly accurate app design/aesthetics for some of the apps also helped immerse me, and I found myself very endeared to Anna and Ashley. This game is no masterpiece, but it's alright for what it is. I'd recommend you play it with a couple friends on voice call - y'all will have a good time leaving nonsense comments on the Jabbr posts, bullying Greg, being irked by Taylor, and making a bizarre dating profile!

review_text_raw:
[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

review_text_raw:
Such a creative horror game!
A phone is left on your doorstep. Like the kind stranger you are, you unlock it to start looking for the owner, but it becomes obvious really quickly that something is wrong...

This game is great because it hooks you right from the start, but it has some flaws. The good things first: The story is very interesting. The entire mystery of where anna is and why the phone is doing the stuff its doing is captivating. Having to puzzle together stuff like passwords from info on the phone is fun, and the athmosphere when playing with headphones is also great, the ambience noises like knocking or someone breathing down your neck all of a sudden sound so realistic It starteled me a few times. Multipe endings also give it replayability.

Now the bad. While for the most part the game does not rely on jumpscares it has some. Not the worst thing, but it jumpscares feel cheap compared to the rest of the atmosphere. The acting. Idk if it was supposed to feel so campy, but it really did (an exeption here would be [spoiler] the simulacra. I really enjoyed the voice acting for it [/spoiler]. And last but not least the characters. You will mostly be interacting with 2 guys, Greg, who is a absolute cunt, and Tylor, who is less bad then Greg but still a creep. Other characters show up but more breifly, so those two are your main "companions". This is fine for the most part, you basically work with them for the greater good to find Anna, but what kind of pissed me off was that you [spoiler] HAVE to be nice to Taylor and trust him to unlock the only good ending. This guy is NOT trustworthy [/spoiler]

Still had a BLAST with it and would reccomend playing it!

Caveat: I played this in English.
The idea of this isn't new; in fact I've played others like Replica and A Lost Phone. I really wanted to like this one, but I don't think I can recommend it. I think the writing is pretty bad, the chat conversations interrupt too much, and the puzzles are not fulfilling. Because the English is weird, the minigame where you choose the words in order to make a sentence was a bit of a crapshoot because there was phrasing used in it that wasn't natural. That's true for the whole game. The video and audio portions are a lot better, but the text (which is most of the game) is weak.
It's not expensive so I'm not asking for a refund, but I don't think it's a good version of this type of game.

review_text_raw: This is definitely a game you play only a couple of times, but when you do it's long and great. The overall lore that makes up the game is extremely interesting in my opinion, and the careful framing of character interactions and their definitions make them memorable overall. My personal favorite part was hunting for all the endings and secret easter eggs. Only thing that I didn't really like was the lack of save points. Endings are arguably the most important parts of the game, yet you are forced to restart from the very beginning after getting an ending. This can be a bit frustrating when you chose the wrong option and got an ending that you already have. The game does give you a faster experience where the text goes faster after achieving your first ending, however I feel like a save point would make more sense in this case.

I found the game interesting and would have loved to see it through,but i couldn't bring myself to finish it.

In other reviews it's mention that it might be a bit of a slog to get through,but i found the information gathering,while repetitive to be quite nice and clever.

What stops me if the sudden jumpscars,they are not telegraphed well (there is very little to no indication that a jumpscared will happen,no tension build up,none of that,one moment you are looking through apps and suddenly you're struck with a jumpsacre when returning to the homepage).

As someone who is quite sensitive to jumpscares,even already knowing about the fact that there were jumpscares,the first major one was what stopped me from wanting to play.If the jumpscares were more subtle and less horrific i think it would have been more possible for me to finish,or at least get further in.

Another issue i had was that the game had no way of changing the volume inside the game,and i had to change it manually on my computer,someone who is less technically literate would probably have gotten an unintended jumpscare from the sudden volume from purely opening the game

The voice acting (with greg specifically) any many dialog was unrealistic,but i foudn it to be a more enjoyable part of the game,as they contrasted the poorly executed jumpscares in levity,though i would understand if it was not the intended effect.

it is truly a shame,because using the mediums and technology for this kind of horror would have been truly wonderful,clever and thought provoking,and even if nihilistic,the story  (as far as i have heard in other's videos and such) and how it applies it's title to it's themes could have been great.

i might look into it's sequals,but i may simply not have the stomach to actually go through on playing them,i hope you have a lovely day :D

review_text_raw:
[h1]👍 Highly Recommended[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA is one of the few games that genuinely makes browsing through a smartphone feel fun. It's a horror game of sorts, but Instead of running from monsters or hiding in closets, you're piecing together the disappearance of a young woman by exploring every corner of her phone. Messages, photos, videos, emails, social media, and browser history slowly reveal a mystery that's equal parts psychological thriller and supernatural horror. It feels disturbingly believable-almost like scrolling through someone else's real device.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🟢 PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Brilliant Found Phone Concept:[/b] Investigating an entire mystery through a lost smartphone is an incredibly immersive idea that still feels unique years after release.
[*][b]Excellent Storytelling:[/b] The narrative unfolds naturally through text messages, emails, videos, and social media instead of lengthy exposition. Every app contains another piece of the puzzle.
[*][b]Convincing Characters:[/b] Conversations feel surprisingly authentic. Friends, coworkers, and family all have believable personalities and motivations, making the investigation feel personal.
[*][b]Genuinely Creepy:[/b] SIMULACRA builds tension through unsettling discoveries, disturbing videos, and the feeling that something is deeply wrong with the phone itself.
[*][b]Creative Puzzles:[/b] Unlocking files, recovering deleted data, solving passwords, and navigating fake apps keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.
[*][b]Multiple Endings:[/b] Your decisions matter, giving the story additional replay value.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]🔴 CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Live-Action Acting Can Be Uneven:[/b] Most performances are convincing, but a handful of scenes feel slightly awkward compared to the otherwise strong production.
[*][b]Occasional Interface Frustrations:[/b] Searching through apps or revisiting conversations can sometimes be more cumbersome than necessary.
[*][b]The Ending May Divide Players:[/b] Without spoilers, the final revelations won't satisfy everyone, especially those hoping for a more grounded explanation.
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]💰 VALUE FOR MONEY[/h2]
[b]Excellent[/b] — SIMULACRA offers several hours of engaging investigation packed with memorable moments, clever puzzles, and one of the most original horror concepts in the genre. It's frequently discounted on Steam, making it an even easier recommendation for fans of narrative adventures and psychological horror.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]⭐ 9/10[/h3]
[i]A brilliantly executed smartphone horror that proves the scariest place in a horror game isn't an abandoned mansion. Immersive, unsettling, and remarkably original, SIMULACRA remains one of the most engaging narrative horror experiences available on Steam.[/i]

review_text_raw:
The story was nothing if not cliché. The concept of a found phone game is cool, or perhaps was at the time of release, but everything else surrounding this concept left me quite underwhelmed.

So many of the characters are creeps, and I find out I got the bad ending for not helping out either of the creeps continue their creep life.
This game also falls into the pitfall of any visual novel type game, it feels stricly linear and there doesn't feel like theres much you can do to change the outcome of the game. Of course this isn't entirely true; there are mutliple endings. But the steps you have to take to get the endings are either vague or require you to work with the aforementioned creeps to save a woman who shouldn't be placed in these creeps crosshairs.

Also what's the message of this game, that putting on an online persona is bad? Sure, maybe, but we see one character using a persona to her benefit?
Is it that forming relationships online is bad? Sure, they can be. But again; there are benefits to forming relationships online too.

The main villian of the game, if you could call it that, doesn't really have a solid theme. Is it AI? Something paranormal? Eldritch horror? A mix of them all plus more?
Even with this in mind, why make it a supernatural entity? Why can't the villian just be a normal guy, like what happens in real life. It feels like meta commentary for meta commentary sake. 

This is the kind of game I suspect would do well in a youtuber letsplay, it's something to be watched and commentated on. I suspect this because I only really had fun with this game because I was playing it with my friends.

As for the "horror" aspect, its a bit of a joke. Loud noises or random unexpected noises playing at random times - most egregiously "door knocking sfx"

Wouldn't reccomend, but its cheap so do as you will.

review_text_raw:
If you have ever wondered how ugly it could get in the event that AI were to take over, well, this game depicts one possible reality. 

Enjoyed it overall, but aiming to reach 100% completion left me with mixed feelings.


Simulacra is a modern take on a philosophical idea that originated in an essay called "Simulacra and Simulation" from 1981. It's simple, and yet, if you manage to reach any ending, and the true ending especially, you will likely ask yourself questions about how you approach your existence in our digitalised world.

The game has its flaws, but if you're okay with this format, then you will probably have a good time.


When I played Simulacra for the first time in 2018, I played it, and I enjoyed it a lot. I was impressed by the simplistic yet effective nature of the storytelling that was made relevant due to the then technologically transitional period: everyone learning how to use smartphones for almost anything. I also appreciated how little the game requires of you, safe for the patience to read, comprehend, observe, and stop to think for a moment, making it an easy recommendation for playing after a mentally and physically demanding day.

That was then. But what about now...?


Lately, I had been thinking a lot about the topics of Simulacra, Simulation, Simulacrum, and AI, so I decided to replay the game and complete it because I liked it so much my first time. It took me 2 playthroughs to reach completion. The first one took 4-5 hours, and the second - no more than 2-3. My recommendation if you were to seek completion within the day would be to do it with a guide next to you. Some achievements, especially the hidden one and the true ending, require noticing and doing a number of things, which could take you hours to nail by going back again and again -- which could be enjoyable if you're into that and are okay with spending more time with the game.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

review_text_raw:
[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options. 

All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?". 

For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

Unfortunately, the game still suffers from the on-rail feel of SIM.  This stems from what seems to be an idiot protagonist: like  in SIM, many times the options the players are given are all stupid or outright needlessly antagonistic toward allies.  While a protagonist who is too genre-aware would be bad, I would prefer to be able to play a character closer to my headspace than  the often cluelessly bumbling protagonist.

Still, the game has a wonderful presentation and is fun for an inexpensive thriller.  I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a neat way to spend part of an afternoon.

I'm surprised. I was expecting something maybe a little hokey or cheesy by the end but what I got was actually a surprisingly effective, creepy tech horror story.

It feels like it wouldn't be out of place as something from the first couple of V/H/S movies. It apes the whole unconventional found footage thing to a tee and despite the occasional spot of grammatical weirdness, it's extremely well made and polished, especially for like five bucks. The acting was reasonably good, the villain was out and out creepy and well done. You can't ask for more, really.

It's about the perfect length for this sort of thing (two to three hours), there's a few puzzles that take some thinking but nothing that's complete and utter nonsense logic and it's replayable and branching with plenty of hidden easter eggs. Kudos to the developers, I'm glad I found out this was a thing.

I really don't want to spoil this game for anyone, so I am just going to encourage you to do one thing : just buy SIMULACRA and play it through for yourself. For such a low price I don't think it is a very risky investment, and if you are interested in narration in video games it could be a shame to miss it.

I wouldn't say it's a perfect game, there is still room for improvement, especialy in how the game handles the player doing things out of order. But I would lie if I didn't say that I was glued to my screen from start to finish. Video games are truly different from non-interactive art forms, but sometimes it takes a game like SIMULACRA to remind us of it. To remind us that video games can create experiences that have never been made possible before.

Despite some flaws, this game is a truly unique experience that I would encourage you to experience.  And to maybe leave a review when you are done with it, even if you didn't like it. Because I firmly believe that this is one of those games that can push the medium forward.

review_text_raw:
I was pretty impressed with Sarah is Missing when it came out, though it definitely had its flaws. With Simulacra, the developers have clearly built on criticisms of their first game and made for a way more unsettling and entertaining experience. 

The game does rely a bit on jumpscares at times, but not to an excessive or obnoxious degree. Far better is what the game does with subtle ambiant spookiness--things that happen in the background that don't really draw attention to themselves but definitely left me feeling unsettled. 

There are still some things that didn't work for me. The corrupted images and messages were fun, but a little bit too easy, and often didn't really give a satisfying payoff. review_text_raw:
At the time of its release, I was kind of obsessed with Sara is Missing. The style was fresh and new, and what a great idea! Finding a missing person through their phone is already such an interesting mystery, a look at how much of our lives are stored in this technology with a personal touch. However, in the end, I had too many questions that went unanswered, and ultimately felt unsatisfied.

SIMULACRA, on the other hand, has so far fixed all of these issues. For clarity sake, I have only achieved two endings at this time, and have more to go. For the same reason, and to give my respect to the developers, I will say I found this game through NightMind's video. This was one of the very, very few times I actually paused in the middle of a video to go out and buy the game myself - I will admit however, the low price was a factor in that. I was expecting more, but this game was more than worth my money.

There are a few silly little mistakes - Some of which add a level of realism and are undoubtedly intentional, like the varying type styles and occasional grammar errors and misspells... And some which are just a little funny, but in the end, the writing and acting won me over any time I was distracted from the experience. The mystery this time around is far more fun and rewarding to solve, the characters are largely likable (UNLESSANNAWHEREARETHOSEDATAREPORTS) and believable within this context.

The whole theme of using someone's phone to dig through their identity is played with far, FAR more effectively here, and the paranormal aspects (cmon it was obvious) offer some commentary, as well as another interesting character I wanted to explore.

The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over.

There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart.

While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. Or call 911, call her friends, read her texts and emails, waste her phone battery, and etc.

review_text_raw:
I'm too hot
Hot damn

This game's got me heated.

Simulacra is a simulated mobile phone method of delivering a horror game. It is based on the disappearance of a young woman named Anna, and the protagonist (you) has discovered her phone on their doorstep. From there, you delve into the secrets of her phone to find all the information you can, and try to locate--and subsequently save--Anna.

From a mechanical perspective, the game is pretty solid. There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story.

However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results.

Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.

review_text_raw:
This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.

I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.

The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery. 

It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information. 

The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.

I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.

Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

Regardless, I look forward to what Kaigan Games does in the future. The world building for this game was good, until... well.. the end.

review_text_raw:
I'm a huge fan of this kind of voyeuristic mystery genre, and this is one of the best I've come across. 
The mixing of platforms; text, audio and FMV, creates a very realistic and immersive phone to explore. The level of detail inside the phone apps is also unparallelled. You can explore people's profiles on the dating app and strike up a conversation with someone inconsequential, you can read comments on posts on the social media app, you can read spam emails. So much detail was put into building the world.
The characters (while the voice and visual acting can be a little hokey) each have their own distinct personalities through texts and messages, the writing there is spot on, plus you can interact with them in so many different ways it feels like your voice really matters to the plot.   
I was put off this game initially because I'm a huge wimp and not a big horror fan, but the scares never made me want to stop playing, and it was really worth it.
11/10 I can't wait for the next game from these guys.

review_text_raw:
After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game [spoiler]Simulacra[/spoiler] would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.

Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris [spoiler]though of course allusions can be found in the website, thanks to the phone number and Morse Code[/spoiler], was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.

For the devs:
[list]
[*]The ambiance is brilliant.  I love the room behind the phone, the lights flickering and the sounds around me.  It definitely creates an aura of suspense.
[*]As far as jump scares, I agree with Night Mind, unnecessary, kind of lame, and ineffective.
[*]What did solving the puzzles accomplish?  I mean, I don't know if I had to unscramble the photos and texts to progress, I just always do it to get it out of the way, but they don't, in the story, progress anything, really, [spoiler]until the Spark conversation with James[/spoiler].  Also they were really easy.  When you present me with a four-word scramble...come on.
[*]Where is this supposed to take place?  The accents were peculiar.  It seemed like you were aiming for American, but you were using British spellings, i.e. favourite.  Is it meant to take place in Canada?
[*]I did love the multiple endings, and felt much more invested in them than I did in SiM.  In particular, [spoiler]I just achieved the happy ending, and afterward, stared at the screen and said, "Did I just get possessed?  I think I just got possessed."[/spoiler]
[*][spoiler]Even if you're interviewing through text (for reasons?), why would you consider hiring a person to be a copywriter who makes that many spelling and grammatical errors?  I kept looking at my response options, and they were painful.  Yes, I understand you're not really applying and just trying to get information about James, but still.[/spoiler]
[/list]
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if [spoiler]the final image had been the player lowering the screen and something vague and shadowy, or even a representation of the Simulacra, being there, and then moving toward the screen if you simply must jump scare, it would have been better than the shift in Anna's picture.[/spoiler]  It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.

Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

review_text_raw:
Overall, I do like the concept behind Simulacra, it gave me a lot of flashbacks to a game called Orwell which also had a very voyeristic/technological vibe and left me wanting to explore more and learn more about the people I was encountering.

However, I have one single criticism of this game based on my experience so far that I think has somewhat soured my opinion of what otherwise seems to be a great horror title with a novel concept, that being the jump scares.

They're completely unessercary and feel rather out of place, the situation the game presents you with is already creepy and uncomfortable enough on it's own without needing to throw up distorted pictures with loud bursts of white noise, it didn't draw me deeper into the experience, it actually yanked me firmly out of it and discouraged me from further exploring the various areas of the phone and probing for more details and information (seeing as I'm not particularly fond of jump scares and random exploration seems like a good way to stumble upon them).

I'd say if someone was going to make another game in this style, have confidence that your concept is creepy enough to draw people in, it'd make a nice change to see more horror titles content to let their horror have a slow, deep burn rather than a quick, short lived flash.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]Genre: Found Phone Adventure/Horror-ish
Time: ~3 hour[/b][/h1]

The player's unnamed character finds a phone on his/her front door, a phone belonging to a woman named Anna. On her phone, there's this weird video of her, making no sense in her speech. After this, you get contacted by different people connected to Anna and the search for what has happened and why the phone landed at your front door can begin.

The phone in itself is quite simple, you've got a phone in front of you, you maneuver it like any other Android phone out there, going through text messages, email, a Tinder clone, a Twitter clone and other apps, in order to find clues as to what has happened. Here and there, you come across a video or a voice message, which also helps to bring the story forward. The only thing I can't really agree on is that people has called it a "horror" game. Maybe I'm just not easily scared, but horror...? Not a chance.

Overall, a pretty good and relaxing game which takes about three hours to complete, but then again... I only finished the game once. There's supposed to be multiple endings and there are some achievements you can hunt through multiple playthroughs just as well.

review_text_raw:
This is more of a meh than a thumb up, but this will have to do.

The story is decent, the game is more or less well executed. There are several annoyances and bugs that can piss you off severely, but nothing game breaking. Although it sports 4-5 endings, there's not much in terms of replayability, and the only replayability you'll find is you going back trying to unlock different stuff, although very little changes in terms of narrative.

On the technical side, the PC port kind of sucks in several aspects: tabbing doesn't move you through different textboxes, backspacing erases entire words, the sound is MIND NUMBINGLY HIGH and there is no volume slider anywhere to be found (I literally played at 1/100 volume with my headphones, and it almost did my head in), occasional bugs with event music not stopping (yay, the screeches and white noises!) or completely freezing (yay, the kill & restarts!).

With that being said the first playthrough is quite enjoyable, and the game is rather cheap, so I couldn't not recommend it. Although I'd still bash the damned phone screen on every voice dialogue or unskippable video (me having to trial and error 7-8 entire playthroughs didn't help, probably). Hopefully it will get fixed in the future or in eventual future iterations of the game.

review_text_raw:
When you are a mature person and your childhood and carefree days are already over, you have kinda stressful job, you don't feel like playing hard games, or games where you have to concentrate a lot. Sometimes, you just want to come over to your place. make yourself a cup of tea and just relax on comfortable chair and just enjoy some kinda easy game. Preferably, with a mouse only controls.

But to be honest, you need to be ready that games will be strange, or better call them weird or maybe even creepy in some kinda way, cause variety of the titles, that can be played with mouse only is pretty limited and you should expect only chinese visual novels, or some nonsense clickers, or easy tower defense games, or some puzzle logic games.

Or it can be a game like Simulacra. I am not even sure how to call this genre, but what I really do know for sure - this game is completely stupid :) But, in a good funny way. They call it a simulation game, which is kinda fair, but doesn't cover the whole idea of this game. 

So, you start the game playing as not a man, not a woman, just whoever the hell you are, sex is not specified in this game. You found a smartphone and this is where the whole stupid part is about to start. I mean like, imagine you are that person who found a phone, okay? What you gonna do? For me it's completely obvious and easy - if phone is unlockable, you simply need to find someone with a name Mom, Dad, Sister, Boyfriend, Dog in a contact list, call one of them and let them know that you found this device and return it as soon as possible. In case phone is locked, you just need to go to the police station and give it to them for the further actions. Easy as that, don't you think so? But not for our protagonist! Instead all of this, he/she decides to play around with this phone and read messages/mail, check web history, tinder-alike app - I mean like literally everything what you don't have to do, when you find someone's phone, cause this is simply embarassing. For the whole game I had that feeling that I was playing as a retard, who had no job, no personal life, no entertainment sources, literally nothing, so that phone was a greatest relief ever. 

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea.

However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. 

So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you: 

+ Feel like playing some easy game, where is no need for high concentration
+ Are a Black Mirror TV show fan and like all this paranoic idea about how it can be bad somewhere in the future for us with all these high-tech devices
+ Don't agree with me, that carrying a phone to the police station would be the best idea in this situation :)
+ Just looking for a new experience

Avoid this game if you:

- Don't like illogical games, with a stupid protagonist who has no idea what the hell is he doing 
- Have no desire to try something new and unusual

Enjoy!

review_text_raw:
This game has a pretty powerful story. A very GOOD one at that. 
If you take the time to go through everything, read everything, pay close attention. you can expect at least a good 5-8 hours of gameplay, It sucks you in out of curiosity. 
The choices you make may not be the best one even if you think it is. honestly i almost cried a little at the end if not at the same time a bit horrified.  

Throughout the gameplay there had been several moments of intense psychological fear, that is, pending on your definition of what "fear" is to you, this game will absolutely Tap into your Head one way or another!
The unknown is what makes you curious & dig deeper, you will have choices of extreme moral dilemmas, it will make you question yourself. it will make you question others, you'll think twice and three times more. with multiple endings, multiple choices, there are many ways to play this game, there are many directions to go and it may not play out the same as you might see on others game plays such as you tube etc. 

 The best part of the entire game was the build up, terrifying sounds that had me literally shaking & taking a break for a good 10 minutes, there are moments of silence and sudden disturbing yet harmless interruptions. 

Overall, between the puzzles & stumped moments, frights, jump-scares, humor etc, there is NOTHING i didn't like about this game. 
I HIGHLY recommend purchasing it & i HIGHLY recommend playing it more than once!  The devs did a spectacular job building this game based on Simulacrum, Simulation & Hyperreality.  bravo.

now that it's complete, I need to sit in a fetal position & think about what I've done.
PS. keep a pen & paper with you.  it will come in handy

review_text_raw:
I must admit. I really REALLY enjoyed playing this game.

When I first saw the tag 'Horror', I was a little scared to play this. I'm not a fan of things that scare me, but I managed to get through this and had a blast. *There are a couple jumpscares obviously because why not XD* (I legit flip out at them and tell them to screw off haha)

So in short, Simulacra is about a girl named Anna who has gone missing, and you have to dig through information through her apps, photos, friends, and even people outside of her circle, in order to find out what the hell happened to her.

And I mean you have to dig through a lot of information sometimes.

However, it's not to say that it wasn't fun doing a treasure hunt. Whenever I figured out how to solve one of the tasks based on the information found in different apps, I felt overjoyed. This game makes you really look for the clues where it makes sense.

Also, by the end of the game, I almost felt like I knew the characters. They were very believable, and that's what really connected with me.

Overall, I just love the idea of using solely a phone. It creates a constraint, allowing for so many possibilities and new ways to create and solve puzzles.

I can say that I have only a couple complaints though.

1) When you look through Anna's message history, you come upon these special messages that are in complete disarray. In order to understand what it said, you had to rearrange the words to fix the message. Sometimes, it was just really difficult for me to figure out what that sentence was. I sometimes maybe spent a little too much time and couldn't progress until I figured it out. Most of the messages weren't important enough to do this, except for one. To be honest, I'm probably just not very good at it.

I only really decrypted those messages for my own curiosity, but because they weren't extremely important except for the story-important ones, there was no huge incentive to decode them.

2) While I do like treasure hunting for those sweet juicy clues in the phone data, sometimes the hints are a little too subtle. I'm not extremely great at puzzle games, so I'll miss details, whether they are obvious or not. I think I took a break because I spent so much time trying to figure out something that was so obvious because I simply missed the detail in a sea of texts. Not a big issue, but I just wanted to point that out for the average gamer playing this. I mean I had to look up something once, so it's not bad on my end.

All in all, this game was just amazing, and I look forward to see what's next :D

(Seriously though. I recommend playing this without any spoilers. This was an amazing experience, and it was a good price for such a wonderful story)
