I don't often play games that genuinely keep me tense and engaged all the way through; but this has got to be one of them. This is modern, internet-age horror done right, and it evokes way more atmosphere and tension than you'd expect from its simple interface. And it's all wrapped up in a statement about the role that smartphones and social media play in our modern lives that's genuine without being preachy.

It's not perfect, of course - the most obvious flaw being some VERY hit-or-miss voice acting - but the flaws rarely inhibit the overall experience. On the whole, this is a must for horror fans, and I really can't wait to see what these devs do next.

- Story is gripping, twists are fun although some are quite predictable
- Atmosphere is strong, with the right feelings of paranoia and eerieness.

- Character list kept short, but with a lot of personality
- Choices matter

- The endings are either far too vague to properly understand, or too deep to easily understand. I can't tell which, but I didn't get as much from it as I hoped.
- If you accidentally mis-click a dialogue option, or you do something else dumb, there's a good chance you're gonna need to restart the entire game to rectify it. This is also true of endings, so you'd better be prepared to replay the game at least 3 times.

review_text_raw:
A psychological horror/mystery about invading others privacy and cyberstalking?  Talk about checking all my boxes at once!  I'm in!!!

Okay, so this is a little game about you having someone elses cellphone.  I beat it in a few hours, four maybe, and enjoyed the trip.  Everything you have to do in this game, you do with this cell phone.  You get to break into email accounts, search online registries for sex offenders, and catfish people, all in an attempt to find the ultimate truth.  It's like someone finally based a game off my hobbies.

So, the story is kind of linear, in that you work to unlock new areas of the mystery, piece by piece.  First, you get to play with texts and pictures, then you get enough information to open the email, then you can gather what you need to beat security questions...  I'd say the gameplay is about sifting through information to find what you need to move on.  You also get to talk to the phone owner's friends, and they help to move the plot along, or you can ask them for help if you get stuck.

I say it's linear, but there are actually several branching paths that probably all end up in the same place.  Do you know Telltale games?  Kind of like that...  We might make a different turn here and there, but we're all on the same road with a beginning, middle and end.  Example?  Okay, here's an example...  You need to find out some information from this person through text.  Do you own up, tell them you're a creepo reading through someone elses phone because they might be in trouble, or do you try to bluff your way through, pretending to be who you're not?  Make your choice and either way, life will go on.  I don't think you can get stuck.  Then at the end they have a nice little screen that says things like "You and 68% of players looked at the porn stash," just like a Telltale game.  (there was no porn stash...)

It's pretty creative storywise, and I'm not going to give anything away, but it looked like there were about 4 different endings, and I wouldn't be adverse to trying again sometime to see how things can change.  I only had two of them available to me, so I must have needed to do something else to unlock the others, and I'm not entirely sure what that is, which is good to me.  Means the game still has more meat to it.  It reminded me of another game I played called Her Story, and I didn't recommend that one because one play is all it's good for, but this one was more than double the length and I'd be happy to go again some day.

Scariness, it wasn't scary, but I'm pretty tough to phase.  It likes to make creepy noises in your headphones.  There's some image distortion, but I wouldn't call anything a jump scare, which is good, because those turn people off.

TL:DR I had fun.  Maybe you'll have fun too?  I hope I've given you enough information to know if you'll enjoy it too.  That's why I'm writing all this after all.

review_text_raw:
The first playthrough is the most fun because you get to explore the game's limits and be a catfishing detective, although the replay value is pretty low for me because then you realize just how short it really is. For $5 though, it is acceptable. The buildup is great and the ending is decent and not what I expected, but pretty original in its own way. I also think they did a great job with the interface and laid out relatively natural methods for you to do your investigating. The journey was definitely better than the destination for me.

I am a fan of interactive storytelling, but the only thing you really feel invested in is finding out what happened to Anna, and if you're sympathetic, wanting to save her, since she is the only character you really get to know through all your interactions and discoveries. The biggest con for me is that the acting and voice acting was okay at best - at times a little too animated/forced - and I felt if there were more development for the characters, the attachment would truly tear us apart as we are forced to make more choices. Also, the creep factor disappeared for me personally once I got through to the ending.

Overall, I do recommend the game, but not very enthusiastically. It was good, but has a lot of potential to be even better.

review_text_raw:
I absolutely love both games that come with uncovering lore and mystery as well as characters you can really deeply care for, even if you're mostly contacting them through text.
Simulacra is definitely a story game over a gameplay game -- most of the controls are point and click and most of the "game type" puzzles are rather simple. Simulacra really shines through in its story -- uncovering the overarching mystery behind the disappearance of the phone's original owner, Anna. The game also has replayability with four different endings (Though I've only seen two of them thus far), that change with your actions throughout the game.

Probably my only complaint would be that some of the calls and voice messages can have a bit of hokey acting in them, which can draw you out of the game a bit (Except for Taylor, his actor is pretty awesome).

Overall I'd definitely say it's well worth the price if you're looking for an interesting modern mystery to settle down with, as well as a few spooks now and then.

The story was engaging to the point of a novel worthy "couldn't put it down" feel. I had to know what was going on and what would happen to the characters involved. Somehow it managed to create an incredible atmosphere that I would not have credited a game that takes place on a mobile phone as being capable of. 

Simulacra kept me guessing till the end. It also has replay value because your choices matter and there is more than one way for this game to end based on the choices you make. 

For the price it can't be faulted and I would have paid more. The best way to play this is on your mobile phone, but I played the first time on my PC and  found it just as immersive. 

This game will not treat you like a child and it will not hold your hand. You will have to think and you will have to figure things out.

OK, I have just finished one run and I would recommend it!
In shorts,

Goods:
+Lots of contents, even some random guys on Spark, very detailed characterized even for minor characters
+Climax just bumped into at the right moments
+Innovative gameplay rather than just points and clicks
+Real action characters make the game much more immersive
+There are just right amount of minigames beside pure text reading
+Spot on the mentality that people like to check on others' phones and see what're inside, eg. Gallery, videos, etc
+Low price tag!

Bads:
-I can't say Anna is poor at acting, she's good, but she's kind of zoned out during the first second of most of the clips. It looks like that she is thinking what to say then starts acting after one second
-Some unnecessary jumpscares, the script is good, the story is good, come on, you can make the atmosphere scary without cheap jumpscares, make it more subtle, eg. Anna's wallpaper is changing after certain stages, which is spooky and good
-The ending is not so good... The whole process is great but when it comes to the ending... I am ok with the setting but it would be great if the ending part was made longer

review_text_raw:
I really don't like Steam's binary review system. I feel like "some" people would like this game... but to me it's suffering the following:

[list]
[*]Imbalance between (unintended?) camp and "horror" (mostly to do with a couple V/O performances)
[*]EXTREME over-reliance on jump-scares (which takes away from the investigation/mystery aspect)
[*]Some rough writing here and there
[*]Some "simulated choice" options (i.e. you HAVE to say things even if you wouldn't want to or it wouldn't make sense for your character to)
[*]Some REALLY obscure puzzles that have had to be answered by the developers themselves

All-in-all it's not a "bad" game... but it's a great "idea" with some execution misses.

That being said, if you love jump-scares and some weird screwed up imagery with "INTENSE" sound effects, etc. then you might dig this. If I were to arm-chair develop this, I would have held back on some of the jump scares to make them more effective than just annyoing, and leaned more into the "missing person investigation" aspect of things vs. bringing in the [spoiler]supernatural[/spoiler] elements so quickly. 

I think the overall presentation and mechanics are solid... none of my critiques of this game are "budget-related," but more about writing/pacing/etc. 

I'm gonna give this a "no" but with a big caveat, that I wouldn't recommend it to MOST people... I really think something special and unique is buried under the surface of this game, but I think maybe the development team just got a little to shy of the story itself and decided to overload it with trope-y jumpscare image-horror to cover it up a bit. 

I know these games are made by real people, and I empathize with the team behind this and hope they know that my "negative" review comes with a healthy does of optimisim that they have something great in them and look forward to their next go of it!

review_text_raw:
An extremely interesting experience that goes a bit south near the end. 

Simulacra takes place entirely on the phone of Anna, a missing young woman. The player is in posession of her phone, trying to solve the mystery of her disappearance by talking to her friends and enemies, and logging into her various social media accounts. You never know who you can trust, and there's a menacing supernatural element in the background that builds suspense. 

This is all extremely compelling, and it was hard to stop playing- however once the truth is revealed and you come face to face with what's responsible, it takes you right out of the game. It's not enough to tarnish the whole experience, but I really wish they had gone in a different direction.

You can replay the game for alternate ending sequences and achievements but the overall story will not change drastically, still it might add in some additional hours of play for completionists.

review_text_raw:
Oh man. How do I even start? This game was very, very intense. Definitely creepy and super interesting. I don't tend to do horror games, but this one seemed like one that could really deliver. 

 If you've read the premise, you know it's about trying to find the owner of the "lost" phone you've somehow come in possession of. I really like the use of technology is this story. It's set up so that the player is essentially working through a cell phone. There are all kinds of ethical situations you find yourself in as well as interacting with the people in this missing person's life. Who do you trust? Who do you tell? Why is crazy stuff starting to happen? It's all really well done. 

Besides the acting being a bit over the top at times and occasionally not having a respose available that I would have liked, this game delivers rather well. It was suspenseful but humorous in places so that it wasn't totally overwhleming. The story's end was a surprise, which was nice. I thought it was well worth the price. Furthermore, it even has a NG+ that lets you speed through the texts faster so that you can try other paths. I have fully completed the game in about 8.5 hours, which may seem short, but it was so enjoyable that I didn't seem to notice. 

I highly recommend this game and look forward to what the developers decide to release next.

review_text_raw:
Okay, so i just finished playing this (took me something like 5 or 6 hours I believe), and I felt compelled to review this game because it's like nothing I've played before. I had never heard of the "found-phone" genre in games before.

First let me say this: if you're a fan of mysteries, riddles, horror, or to be more specific, found-footage horror, then this game is for you! If not, try it anyway lol you just might be surprised.

This game starts out with you booting up a phone that was sent to you (or left on your doorstep, it's not totally cleared up in the story), and when you do it begins to glitch out a little and then these texts start coming in, and well, it just takes off from there...

The basic premise is that the owner of the phone, a girl named Anna, has gone missing and it's up to you (and a couple others along the way) to try to find her. You do this by digging through her phone and reading EVERYTHING, and then communicating with some of her contacts through texts and emails and an online dating app and a twitter-like app.  As things progress you learn that she has dissapeared and it may be connected to other recent dissapearances (but I won't go into more on that because I don't want to ruin the experience for new players).  Eventually, you realize there's a lot more going on than meets the eye.

The game has a very unnerving, intense feeling to it, and is all the better for it.  It has a decent story, some fun little mini games and riddles, a good amount of investigation and some pretty convinging dialogues, and for the REALLY hardcore sleuths out there, it even has some very interesting "easter eggs" hidden in the game that are quite rewarding to find. (I'll give you a hint here, but that's it...morse code, click it :)   )

As for graphics, sound, story, gameplay, etc...well graphics aren't important here as it's basically a phone emulator, the gameplay is as simple as digging through a phone and talking to people and looking stuff up (but you need a brain lol), the story is interesting enough that you really will never get bored in a single playthrough, and apparently it has many different endings so it has replayability there...where this game really shines though is the sound...it's incredible and really really well done.  When you start they recommend you use headphones, and I STRONGLY recommend you take their advice, it's just not the same on speakers, not even close

Anyway, the TL;DR is this:
if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell!

For me it's a 4.5/5

You do this by digging through her phone and reading EVERYTHING, and then communicating with some of her contacts through texts and emails and an online dating app and a twitter-like app. As things progress you learn that she has dissapeared and it may be connected to other recent dissapearances (but I won't go into more on that because I don't want to ruin the experience for new players). Eventually, you realize there's a lot more going on than meets the eye. The game has a very unnerving, intense feeling to it, and is all the better for it. It has a decent story, some fun little mini games and riddles, a good amount of investigation and some pretty convinging dialogues, and for the REALLY hardcore sleuths out there, it even has some very interesting "easter eggs" hidden in the game that are quite rewarding to find. (I'll give you a hint here, but that's it...morse code, click it :) ) As for graphics, sound, story, gameplay, etc...well graphics aren't important here as it's basically a phone emulator, the gameplay is as simple as digging through a phone and talking to people and looking stuff up (but you need a brain lol), the story is interesting enough that you really will never get bored in a single playthrough, and apparently it has many different endings so it has replayability there...where this game really shines though is the sound...it's incredible and really really well done. When you start they recommend you use headphones, and I STRONGLY recommend you take their advice, it's just not the same on speakers, not even close Anyway, the TL;DR is this: if you 're looking for an action title, look elsewhere, but if you're looking for an EXPERIENCE that really makes you feel like you're a part of a mystery that needs to be solved, I can't recommend this highly enough. It's fun as hell! For me it's a 4.5/5

review_text_raw:
!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

I realize I'm a little late to the party. I purchased this game through a humble bundle, but so far it has been well worth the time and money.

Simulacra is an interesting game. I've only played through it once so I don't have much to go on, but the idea of a central protagonist controlling the digital world is very futuresque. I enjoyed the horror overtones, the cinematics, the voice acting, and the story in general. A few gripes I have are that none of the character's are likeable, and the story feels contrived. Moreover, there's no reason to care about Anna aside from the fact she is the victim in the story. I would have enjoyed a more deeply thought out narrative done by a slightly better funded company.

I reccomend this game if you are into overt horror, by which I mean gratuitous jump scares and cheap mutilation. If you are looking for a puzzle/visual novel hybrid, you may also enjoy the game.

review_text_raw:
There's a sub-genre of games that I like to call voyeur sims -- these include walking simulators like Gone Home, strategy-puzzlers like the Orwell games, and story-driven phone-sim games like [b]SIMULACRA[/b].

These voyeur sims fuel something visceral in me by allowing me to be a peeping tom in someone else's life; overcoming personal privacy as a game mechanic is somehow uncomfortably fun, even when the actual gameplay is minimal.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is one of the better voyeur sims and one of the better games I've played this year. Like other phone-sim games like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/523210/A_Normal_Lost_Phone/]A Normal Lost Phone[/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/496890/Replica/]Replica[/url], it starts with a mysterious cell phone, and throughout the game, you unpack its content in a series of puzzle-driven unlocking sequences.

What sets [b]SIMULACRA[/b] apart is its high production value. High quality FMVs, passable and explorable versions of popular social media apps, realistic text logs and emails -- these all make the small, contained world of [b]SIMULACRA[/b] believable and immersive.

This is a great game. Recommended.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone horror game. The premise of the game is that you (the unknown, nameless protagonist – but presumably *you*, the actual player) found a phone out on your front porch that belongs to a woman named Anna. There’s something off about the phone, though; it keeps glitching out, a number of the files on it are messed up, there’s some creepypasta-esque flashes of the screen changing to horrifying images – and of course it quickly becomes evident from the frantic messages you get from her boyfriend that Anna has gone missing.

The game’s basic premise is exploring Anna’s phone. You decrypt some images and text messages via very simple minigames, but most of it is a choices-matter narrative, as you interact with not only Anna’s boyfriend, but a funny guy named Taylor on Spark (a dating/hookup app that *totally* isn’t Tinder) who had been flirting with Anna, as well as messages from Ashley, Anna’s best friend. You browse a few in-game websites, make a few phone calls from phone numbers you find on them and hidden in various images, and gradually unravel the mystery of what happened to Anna over the course of the game.

This is something of a hybrid of a simple puzzle game and Telltale’s sort of narrative storytelling, where you have a list of dialogue choices and they influence how other characters react to you. There is actually a branching narrative – the choices you make actually influence which endings you can access as you try to save Anna, only to discover that things aren’t so easy, and how you treat the characters affects how they interact with you. If you’re a jerk to someone, they won’t trust you and will be a jerk back; if you’re nice to them, they’ll be more trusting. But at the same time, you can lie about who you are to various people in the game, and while sometimes they’ll figure it out, other times you’ll slot right in as a trusted person and be able to get what you need out of them.

Indeed, pretense is a major theme of the game – people aren’t quite who they present themselves to be online, and the fronts they put up often don’t match who they are (or, indeed, who they perceive themselves to be). Is Anna’s boyfriend really still together with her, or did they break up, and is he stalking her? There’s a bunch of sexual predators on Spark – is Taylor one of them? Does Ashley have ulterior motives in her friendship with Anna?

I’d like to say that the biggest flaw with this game is that the resolution is, perhaps, a bit on the nose. While I approve of this new age of horror, and coming up with a new spooky villain, I also didn’t feel like it did a good enough job of reinforcing the manipulation angle of social media, instead simply resorting to outright mind control, which was a lost opportunity.

However, I think the actual largest flaw with this game is that it is just okay. It is a clever idea, and there are some fun conceits in there, but I have to say at the end I was left feeling just lukewarm about it. When I play a game, or finish a game, I want a sense of satisfaction. But this was just sort of an experience I had. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t particularly excellent, either.

If you’ve never played a game like this before, and somehow got this for free or as part of a bundle, it’d be worth a spin to just try out something new. But at the same time, I’m left feeling like it’s hard to recommend that someone go out of their way to experience it, and when I recommend something, I want to actually be able to say to someone “Yes, you should go play this game.”

I wasn’t left with that feeling here, as while it is overall decent, it is all just a little bit flat, and the jump scares don’t manage to really carry the horror of the game very well.

review_text_raw:
A short and cheap game that provides a good afternoon's worth of gameplay for your first playthrough. 

The gameplay is well polished and smooth. The music is sometimes a bit too loud for my tastes but it is not bad. The smartphone interface however is very well made and simulates a more comfortable experience swiping and clicking. 

The plot is predictable and voice acting is a bit poor. But the game is rich in story-telling, whether it is relevant to the main questline or not. There is plenty of content lying around that gives the characters life and personality. While the main story is quite linear, many parts of the game can be revealed in a non-linear fashion. The attention to detail in everything in the phone is rather amazing.

The conversation choices are quite interesting and relatable, but sometimes you are forced into conversations that you don't really want to to continue for the sake of plot advancement. 

Overall a very good game well worth more than its full asking price. Will try again.

review_text_raw:
Ehh....

The story is pretty silly, to be honest. I haven't gotten all of the endings but I don't really feel much desire to. I won't spoil anything but if you're into this sort of thing (Twilight Zone, Black Mirror, etc.) you probably won't be too impressed with the reveal. The game seems convinced that you care about what happens to the characters, but you aren't really given any reason to. Most of them are either rude or only play minor parts. The voice acting varies, but it's mostly pretty poor, certainly a step down after having just played Her Story. I never really felt like I was part of the game's world, since so much of what happened was out of my control and the dialog options rarely were what I actually wanted to say.

That said, there are definitely some enjoyable moments here. The music/sound is good (if a little harsh sometimes) and the visuals were better than I expected. The gameplay was pretty basic, but it was never frustrating. If the game sounds interesting to you, and you haven't already become desensitized to the genre's tropes, you'll probably feel like you got your money's worth, if not much more.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a game about something. I'm not really sure what, since the game is practically foreshadowing its own inability to deliver on its buildup in many places, and the solution to the mystery had me wondering why there even was a mystery to solve, being that it was something which had little to do with anything that exists in the real world (though there is doubtless some deep philosophical meaning behind the Ghost of Facebook Profiles Past throwing someone off a building for not having enough followers on MySpace).
The story is told through a cast of characters, inlcuding, but not limited to: A man who you can convince to commit corporate espionage and B&E in one sentence each, a sex offender who couldn't shut up to save his life, and the girl who went missing, has her entire character arc revealed in chapter one and never gets any more developement aside from us finding out that everything she did was, in fact, understandable, if rude. All of these reserved seats on the short bus are caught up in a missing person case, but have to do it through the player character, who has his own character, and who can't count to his own IQ. The story is told through tweedle dee and tweedle dum figuring out ways to get more evidence, and the protagonist actually doing it.
The dialogue system is both good and bad. It's bad because the dialogue was bootlegged from Fallout 4, and rarely had the thing I wanted to say, and good in that they actaully manage to do more with it than Bethesda ever did. As stated, the two stooges figure out new ways to attack the case and figure things out, and you actaully do it with puzzling that ranges from "good" to "really bad". There are puzzles where you put together images such that htere's no corruption, which I liked,  puzzles where you unscramble sentences, which were rarely necessary but also rarely obnoxious, and there were puzzles where you have an article to draw information from, but the information in the article is more wrong than the information Bill Cosby the 2nd pulls out of thin air.
Don't worry about the horror elements, it's just a few loud noises and distorted images. So we have a game where the horror is token, the story is confusing, and the characters are dumb and/or pricks. It's technically perfectly adequate, but so are virtually all visual novels, and what extra this does amounts to set decoration. 3/10, since someone who is willing to not think too hard might find it artistically brilliant.

The story is well grounded with plenty of depth and character, though 75% of the voice acting was pretty terrible. The puzzles are woven into the story very well, too, and I never found myself getting bored of the sleuthing and digging through this girls phone to find the answers to progress the plot.

In all, a fantastic experience.

Also, I wholly support the game's reccomendation of headphones (but I shan't ruin why!).

review_text_raw:
This game is really boring. It's a bunch of clicking buttons, along with some typing in of answers, and very light puzzle solving.
Really it's the story where the meat of the game is found, and it's extremely sub-par. I dunno if the author is someone who speaks English as a second language, but the writing is very much flawed, and the logical choices in story progression just don't add up. The story and choices are as limited as the writer is, and this one I find very much unenjoyable.

It focused far too much on a relationship that simply wouldn't happen in reality. That girl is way out of his league, and there's no way Greg and Anna would ever have seen each other. In addition the flirtation, and everything to do with interactions between people is extremely awkward. The voice acting reaches levels of cringe, and not the lel cringe lulz, but the physical reaction of cringing.

Everything about this game is mediocre, and I have no idea how it is sitting at "Overwhelmingly Positive". It is so very far from that, and I think this is people with low expectations due to not seeing much of this sort of thing. The bandwagon effect is also a possibility, as well as attraction to the girl, but whatever the reason, this game is not worth a recommendation.

TL;DR: Posting this review to help Steam out, since this game does NOT deserve such praise. Honestly, I would have been annoyed but said screw it if it was at "Very Positive"... but overwhelmingly positive? It literally does nothing new, innovative, or even good. In fact, I'd say the only thing it accomplished was copying things done many times before it in an absolutely terrible way. It was a slog to get through from beginning to end. I can honestly say it combined all the crappiest parts of horror movie trailers, the worst creepypastas and a s****y jigsaw puzzle together in a terrible phone-shaped package that lasted for WAY too long. It was 30 minutes of terrible content somehow stretched into 3 hours. In other words, if you get it in a bundle like me, go ahead and stop playing when you decide the moment is right. It's not going to get better.

Got this from the "Overwhelmingly Positive" Humble Bundle. How in the actual f*** is this game "Overwhelmingly Positive" ????? Kids review bomb awesome games on here all the time, and this managed to survive that for so long? I'm legitimately confused and concerned. Did this game get massive press in some media targeted specifically towards children, and somehow avoid literally everyone else? Did the people who hate it just not care enough to leave a review? Again, were on Steam, so how?????

On a particularly boring night, I played the entire damn thing. The first 5 minutes in I already knew it was going to be terrible, but stupidly I played on, hoping for something redeeming to happen to justify the positive reviews and my time wasted. That obviously didn't happen.

Bad writing, bad puzzles, atrocious "scares" (literally all jumps, flashing images and noises, and even then not a single f***ing one even managed a startled shutter from me, with volume annoyingly high), all set to an all-too-overplayed by now "hey, play this game on this device/OS/form of communication" gimmick that I'm frankly by now beyond tired of game developers using as a replacement for an interesting story/plot/writing (Stories Untold is the most recent game to do it RIGHT AFAIK). It was cool like the first 100 times maybe, but I'm over it.

I also want to point out, I don't think I have EVER seen good writing/plot in a game that has characters communicating through a messaging system, then has every character using terrible grammar, punctuation, etc. It bugs the hell out of me.
1.It's usually inconsistent. Some chatacters just spring in and out of it randomly.
2.We're not all 12. Some people actually care about that kind of stuff, so it doesn't make sense to have EVERYONE at some point talking like the slow, overly emotional kid in class.
3.It isn't 1995 anymore. It's one thing to have every character talk like that when they're using AOL Instant Messenger, but for chrissakes, you actually have to make an EFFORT to screw up grammar the way these characters do on a modern cellphone with autocorrect. Ugh.

review_text_raw:
I really love this game genre, but this specific game wasn't very good in my opinion, for the following reasons:
- Inconsistent plot. The game just makes use of random horror movie tropes, without them making sense in the story.
- Very cringey characters (both due to the bad writing and to the bad acting), ESPECIALLY the two most important characters in the game: the girl you're supposed to find and the ultimate bad guy. That's a real problem, because it makes it very hard to emphatize with the person you're supposed to save, as well as to take the bad guy seriously.
- Random jumpscares make this game feel pretty shallow.
- Very, very often, the choices that are proposed to you seem forced. Basically, you can feel that the game WANTS the story to progress in a specific direction, and doesn't allow you to very simply avoid issues by being reasonable. For example, at some point, you can either tell a very dangerous lie or tell the truth. But if you tell the truth, at no point does the game allow to explain yourself, and therefore the person you told the truth to just reacts badly for no reason. In real life it would have been easy to avoid that issue, but the game doesn't want that. Hence, choices aren't well made, and overall it doesn't feel like you're really making story progress - it actually more feels like you're following the story where it wants you to go.

Still, there also are some good things:
- The phone interface looks pretty realistic, which is at least one immersive thing
- One playthrough is reasonably long (about 4 hours for the first one), especially since the game is very cheap, and there apparently are four different endings. 
- One or two moments in the story were actually pretty interesting, even though they didn't make sense in the grand scheme of things

Overall, I advice against buying this game, as there are many better ones in the same genre; I for example enjoyed Orwell much more, and both its mechanics and thematics are somewhat similar (without the horror movie aspect of it, which is good riddance honestly), but the writing is much better and realistic (and therefore more immersive as well !) and never made me cringe. Still, Simulacra is very cheap, so if you're okay with what I said above, go ahead.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

Where to start? I just finished the game.

But for the rest, great game. Get it if you can.

I really enjoyed this game, a combination of storytelling and puzzles based around a phone found on your doorstep. I've played a couple of 'Lost Phone' games and none delivered quite the same level of creepy interaction that SIMULACRA achieved. 

I wouldn't describe this so much as a horror game but more a thriller (at least with the ending I got). There were enough twists and turns in the story to keep me interested and played through the game in two sittings. I'm really looking forward to playing through again and seeing how I can manipulate the story differently. 

Often FMV feels a little clunky when dropped into games, but this was a perfect example of wise use of the technology to maximum effect. Really great work from the whole team behind this little indie gem. 

9/10

review_text_raw:
SIMULACRA doesn't disappoint! I don't like to watch "Let's Play's" or anything before playing games because they tend to ruin some of the fun and that certainly is the case here. A lot of the complains I read from players is that they knew what was coming ahead of time... I had no idea and some of the things happening in my headphones genuinely terrified me because I legitimately thought they were happening in my house. I won't spoil what they were for anyone who has yet to play.

Still, like Sara is Missing, I think more can be done with this genre. The apps are fun to play with for a few minutes but it becomes apparent pretty quickly how shallow and underdeveloped they are. The dialogue is quite obviously written by someone to whom English is a second language and they didn't have anyone who speaks English proofread it. Lots of obvious typos and grammatical errors kind of took me out of the atmosphere. The voice acting by one of the characters is over the top to the point that it's cringey. The main character, though, is wonderfully acted and I couldn't tell at first that she wasn't actually American.

Overall I recommend this game to anyone into scares. Do yourself a favor and don't watch any gameplay footage because it will spoil a lot of the enjoyment.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is another game within the sara is missing universe. The first game was good but with new additions to a series brings new mechanics and fixes the short commings of the original, does this game do just that? I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is very creepy. Now jumpscares are cheap and something I dont really enjoy but the game has ambient sound effects that are very spooky. Sometimes you may hear nocking at a door or a wisper or see the lights flicker in your field of view. Some are not really strong in spooking the player but the sound effects really sell the horror.

      The plot is good. Now this is pretty much a horror thriller game that delves with a deep mystery. The game throws you for many loops making you question who can you trust and how much information you should provide. You never know who is at the other end of that text message you recieved. The further you go the deeper the rabbit hole goes.

        The gameplay is simplistic. A game having a simplistic gameplay is nothing to fear. This is like playing a tale tell game where you get dialogue options but sometimes it effects the response of other players and the ending. There are branching paths but not many to get more than 2ish playthroughs. Still it is good to see that some choices creates a response that effect the story and feels a bit like a genuine response in a hypothetical world.

Con:
      There are some puzzles that are difficult. This game has quite a few moments that test memory and makes you search for clues to progress but some of these clues are very well hidden meaning in order to progress you might need to search the internet for the solution to save the frustration. It is a minor issue but i swear there is this one puzzle i could never solve.

Conclusion:
       In short this game is short but it is a blast to play. The story is creepy with atmoshere and has a great story. If you play the game for just a short ammount of time you will be hooked into finding out the truth. I can not reccomend this game enough for anything curious in the game. It is resonably priced in retrospect to how long the game is.

review_text_raw:
7.5/10

I don't know how I missed this one when it first came out. I've played a couple of these titles that have you navigating a lost phone (A Normal Lost Phone, Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story, Replica, etc.), and generally find the premise captivating, even if I have some irritations with the details of each game. In addition, SIMULACRA was quite well received on Steam. At the time of this writing, the game has 96% positive reviews overall!

As I began to explore, there was a lot to like about the game. The phone felt "real," and I thought that the Apps that were present were a good reflection of what many young people have installed. I enjoyed the "de-scramble" puzzles that allow you to decrypt texts and photos, although a few of the text puzzles seemed like they should have multiple solutions. Lastly, I thought that the sound design was brilliant. Periodic background sound effects keep the player tense and worried about their exact location while perusing the phone's contents. Lastly, the sound effect recorded by Greg in Anna's home (also used later in the game) is just so unnerving. The game does an excellent job of creating an unsettling tone.

But of course, there were a number of things I didn't like as well. I felt that the game could be a bit too linear during the majority of the playthrough - you often were forced to have dialogue with either Greg or Taylor before the game would progress, even if you weren't particularly interested in talking with them. I thought it felt strange to receive calls on the phone and be unable to answer. Afterwards, the caller would typically ask you by text why you didn't answer, and you typically would respond with something like, "I couldn't understand what you were saying." However, I never felt that I had difficulty understanding what was said - the game just didn't provide me with the means to respond. I want to refrain from spoiling the game for anyone, but the game has something important to say about conformity and romantic desirability in the digital age. Lately, I've gone down a weird rabbit hole of buying/playing cheap games on Steam. When Simulacra popped up, I figured I would give it a try because the "found cell phone" genre is usually entertaining. For an indie game, this was a fun and well-executed romp. I managed to unlock all 24 achievements; having done so, I can say that unlocking each ending can be a bit tedious, because one wrong step can undo all of your hard work. That actually brings me to my other complaint: the game's auto-save feature is really weird and just adds to the tediousness of replays. I wish that we had the option to control saves, as that would have made it easier to replay the game in an attempt to unlock the other endings.

That aside, the game was pretty fun. The acting was a bit cheesy and there were some pretty obvious grammatical errors, but I mean, it's an indie game. All things considered, it was enjoyable and well worth the $2. I don't know why, exactly, but I enjoy these little games where you have to explore someone's life through their cell phone. I'll definitely check out the other games from this developer.

review_text_raw:
I'm a big fan of found-phone games, and had previously enjoyed Sara Is Missing. SIMULACRA is an extension of those horror-tendrils into the tiny genre, and definitely ranks well amidst other contenders like Unrd (Last Seen Online, The Silent Truth, My Last Three Days, Now Live, etc etc), Replica, the Normal Lost Phone series, and so forth. (It should be noted that I also count alternate OS and hacking games in this genre when it allows for entrance into a character's private computer; Mainlining and Orwell definitely contribute to the genre in substantial ways--)

This one has a great narrative pushing it forward, but the big stumbling block comes from the clunky puzzle integration. Content in the phone is corrupted, and appears as fragmented photographs and jumbled up text messages that need your help in piecing back together. These broke the immersion of the game in ways that Normal Lost Phone, Unrd, and Orwell all avoided. Password puzzles were more believable, but I felt that if the developers had added something like 'download a decrypting software' or something like this, and then integrated the gamification/puzzles into that as a feature/way to pass the time, I would've received that far better than the literal piecing-together. Another issue with that was how it forcibly slowed down playthroughs on repeat-plays for the different endings. Despite these extremely minor flaws, the great acting and overall game design definitely proved to be an engaging time-eater. Websites looked and behaved believably, characters were hilarious and genuine, you found yourself caring for Anna amidst all these weirdos. I hope to see the primary antagonist's motivations and development played out over future games, as I don't believe this is the end of their story. Definite thumbs up from me.

review_text_raw:
8/10

A very interesting and well done horror game about fiddling with a stranger's phone.

Before Simulacra, the devs made Sara is Missing, a game following the same line (horror game about exploring someone's phone) and, in Simulacra, it's easy to notice how much the game has evolved. While in SIM there were some choices to be made but ultimately they didn't change all that much, in the case of Simulacra it actually changes, with 4 possible different endings depending on what you do during the game.

The game involves talking to people using the phone's messenger app, browsing through other apps, searching for clues and solving some puzzles, while experiencing some creepy things on the way. The story, although somewhat linear (with some differences based on your choices) is interesting and well done. Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings.

I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person.

Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price.

Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings. I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person. Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price. Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

review_text_raw:
My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

review_text_raw:
A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
A rather short game about a missing person.

You work on the missing persons mobile phone throughout the game and interact with Apps and send messages to persons.
While doing so, through music and ambient sounds, and a scare from time to time, this game creates an extremely intense atmosphere and pulls you into it's world!

Very, very good game. Highly recommend playing it. The 4€ are not much to pay for a couple hours of enjoyment!

I played it for a bit more than 5h now in one day.
In this time I completed my first and therefore truthful to my character playthrough, with a rather satisfying, though not "good" ending.
This took me around 4-4.5h

The remaining time, and time that will add from now on, is used for achivements, since this game let's you have them rather easily by reaching certain optional objectives that are never stated anywhere though ;)
So if you like to get into some secret hunting: This might be a game for you!

At the time of writing this review, I completed 4 out of 5 endings.
All of which are different enought to have their own twist to them! Really nice.

I know what the last ending will result in, but the details are yet unknown.

There are some negative points though, as no game is perfect.

Since we are talking about a "mobile game port" (to my knowledge that is), there are some essentials lacking.

This game features no settings menu of any kind.
It is not possible to lower the audio, except through the OS' sound mixer ...
That is not acceptable, far less in a post TB (TotalBiscuit) world.
Being able to lower Sound, Music and/or Video (which is sparsely used), would make this a more proper PC-game.
Also I haven't seen the possibility to change resolution, though the game is played only on about 10% of the screen anyway (due to the type of game it is ...)

There are subtitles hidden in the help-menu in main menu.

Especially in the later part of the game, the music is a tad too loud in comparison with the voices, so understanding suffers from it.

Other than the just stated? Not much to complain about.
Scrolling is a bit awkward, but works well enough by mousewheel and "dragging" via left click.
Typing in the places necessary is a bit lackluster since backspace deletes the whole last word (which can be a pain for fast typers that want to correct a misstype ...)

THats pretty much it.
Support this awsome dev!

review_text_raw:
[i]Simulacra[/i] is a captivating puzzle-slash-detective-slash-horror-slash-social commentary game which is yours to enjoy for a delightfully economic entree fee.

So you found a phone on your doorstep and it appears to belong to the now missing twenty-something Anna. Your quest to find out what happened to her will take place entirely through the smartphone interface, trying to get into contact with her familiars, sifting through her social media posts and recovering lost files. Soon enough the mysteries start to pile up. Those who have a basic grasp of the philosophy of Jean Baudrillard may already guess what's behind the sudden disappearance.

It's a short game which will take approximately 4-5 hours to finish, which is enough to get involved with the characters while still short enough so that the gameplay does not grow stale. There is replay value to be had, since your decisions (who to trust, what to do) can take the story to different conclusions.

The game touches on a few social issues, such as [spoiler]sexual harassment[/spoiler], [spoiler]the banality of social media content[/spoiler] and [spoiler]the ongoing digitization of society[/spoiler], but I never found the game to be either too preachy or too political. There is also some existential philosophy woven into the dialogues, though it's enough to give you something to muse about, it's too little to be considered profound. The puzzles are fairly easy, making the game more appealing to casual gamers rather than seasoned point-and-click fanatics.

At the bottom of all its qualities are certainly the jump scares. While it can be argued that this much loathed trope does the trick (i.e.: keeping you on edge even during the quiet moments), they are still a cheap substitute for the subtleties of psychological horror. That said, the game did manage to frighten me through the sheer eeriness of a digital device continually distorting into absolute madness, but the rather bland acting in the audio/video files often pulled me out of suspense-belief and back into the comfort zone.

[b][u]Final verdict:[/u] 7/10[/b]. [i]Simulacra[/i] is a fresh and well-executed, though somewhat poorly acted missing person mystery.

review_text_raw:
This game is fun and I recommend it -- it's a good way to kill a few hours and is a bargain even at full price. The interface is fun, the mystery is fun, the suspense and creepiness is fun. But there are some not-fun things.

* the jumpscares are just kind of pointless. There's no reason for them to exist, not even within the narrative itself. They ended up making me roll my eyes. The Game's scariest moments are the ones where you feel a slow dread due to the knowledge you've gained

* the story isn't thematically coherent. it doesn't know what it's trying to say. in the end it makes some claim about the fakeness of social media or w/e, but that's not really supported by the rest of the game, which spends a lot more time with the cause and effect of non-social media-related interactions. That makes the denouement feel dissatisfying, as a lot of stuff, like the conflict with the ex-boyfriend or the relationship with the best friend, feel like they could have been replaced with anything else and the story remain intact, which means they're just window dressing and not even that important. It feels disrespectful to the player and to the characters.

* the game has multiple endings but doesn't let you skip ahead when dialogue is playing! This is the most irritating oversight. I ended up pulling up Cheat Engine on second playthroughs so I could turn up the game's speed so I didn't have to wait so long for the chat bubbles to show up. 

* dialogue looks like it was written by non-native English speakers, and I don't just mean text speak, I mean grammar wise it's awkward. Could stand to see some copy editing.

* just generally a lot of interesting concepts and ideas that get raised but not carried out to their full potential. There's a lot here to like, but a lot of misses in execution. I liked the interface messing directly with the player that happens partway through the game, but then nothing ever comes of it. It could have been totally cut from the game and the story would remain unchanged, which is just a bummer.

But those are my gripes, I still had a fun time, so yeah, buy the game!

review_text_raw:
This is amazing work. Especially considering that it was made by a small dev team. I am an instant fan )

I believe this is the kind of game that is best to go into completely blind (don't even read the description on the store page). Part of the immersion and excitement comes from the fact that you don't know where it's going. Overall expect a good story and well written characters with some light puzzles; mechanically not very different from an adventure game. Definitely worth your time.

Light spoilers follow.

[spoiler]
What impressed me most was the way it breaks the fourth wall. Let me explain. Nowadays a lot of games engage in some kind of meta-commentary, be it lampshading or just generally making jokes or winking at the player. When it's done competently, it can be somewhat amusing.

This game does something else. It actually manages to make the player take responsibility (emotional, moral) for some of the in-game decisions. It's probably hit and miss, but there were a few moments where I was really compelled to question my judgement. Did *I* decide to do this? What does it say about me as a person? And after the game tricks you into doing something questionable, it slaps you with an achievement on top of it ) For me this was where it really shined.
[/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
This game is really fun to play and playing it scared me from time to time, more than probably watching any horror movie. So tl;dr: if you are interested in exploring through stuff in a spooky mood, play it.
There is a lot to mention when it comes to all the good part this game has. Probably, most of them are mentioned in the other comments but basically:
-A catchy start
-Great experience with headphones
-For a simple game, it is visually pleasing
-Actors who were involved are not bad at all
-If you are not dumb, probably you will not be stuck and be disconnected from the journey while digging through the puzzles, it kinda carries a good balance unlike the most game with the same genre
The list could go on and on. Although I enjoyed the game a lot, there are three minor things I'd like to mention, which I think could be better. 
The first is storywise. The story grows really great and creates so many expectations(especially because of the name "Simulacra"), but the ending is just not as strong as I expected. If you actually do know what this whole "Simulacra" thing is about(especially read the book Simulacra and Simulation by Jean Baudrillard), you just find the ending a little bit cheesy. No offense but, I think it could have been written way better. 
Secondly, the puzzles could be a little harder, just a little bit. I am aware that with this, it does not get in front of the story but you just expect one or two puzzles that could really challenge you. Yet, there is none. 
Lastly(this is a bit spoiler do not read this part unless you played it), I think it could have been better if the game also included the possibility of making the player believe or think that the whole plot could actually be a kidnapping(by Greg or Taylor) because I think, this would really improve the game. With no consideration of possible kidnapping scenarios, some dialogue options are so dead to choose(like you never believe that Taylor or Greg are somehow involved, so you are unlikely to accuse them).
These are just my humble opinions, nonetheless, I enjoyed the game a LOT! Thanks to anyone who were involved in creating this beautiful game. A great experience, nicely done!

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is essentially a mixture of a horror-adventure and an epistolary novel. Its almost like an Alternate Reality Game, but it takes place in a fake internet, accessed through a fake cellphone. 

This is a very interesting method of depicting the story, and it comes with its own natural puzzle aspects that make it suited for a casual adventure game. 

The music is atmospheric. The plotline is pretty enjoyable, and believably written. Its creepy, and a good horror experience.

PROS
+ Atmospheric
+ Interesting presentation that has its own inherent mechanical aspects, thus making the gameplay feel natural
+ Very engaging

CONS
- Not a big challenge, nor the longest or deepest game out there.

OVERALL
An enjoyable casual horror-adventure. Atmospheric, creepy, and nicely presented. Absolutely recommended for fans of horror, fans of adventure games, fans of visual novels, and fans of experimental narrative games (aka "walking sims").

review_text_raw:
Just finished my first playthrough and I can say I really liked the game and I think it totally worth the full price. The premise is original and simple (in a good way): check out an apparently missing person phone's and try to figure out what has happened to her.

In gameplay terms this translates to a visual novel+puzzle solving mash-up. Not that I considerer this a bad thing at all, quite the opossite I think it allows to put emphasis on a strong branching narrative.

I found it easy to "put myself in character" since the game revolves around interacting with the phone's apps and the story tackles on some contemporary problems -like whom you can trust on a social network, how much of info you should share, sexual harrasment, etc-. I know is not the first game that deals with many of these issues: I can recall Orwell but in that case the tone is more scify/conspiracy theory while here's more intimate and gradually turns to horror.
Since I don't want to spoil anything of the story all I'm saying is that the first playthrough took me almost four hours, horror elements are introduced without overdoing it (although some people may argue that they're kinda jump scares if the game hooks you like it happened to me it can be unsettling) and I think it's worth at least a second playthrough to get a different ending.

[i]Go for it if:[/i]
[list]
[*] you're into psychological horror
[*] you have no problem reading "a lot"
[*] you're curious about how text-adventures could evolve
[/list]

[i]Stay away if:[/i]
[list]
[*] you expect a survival horror or an action oriented horror themed game
[*] you're exclusively into complex mechanics/systems
[/list]

This is a decent "choices matter" voyeuristic psychological thriller with the occasional horror elements (jump scares) that is a must play for horror fans and might be worth checking out on sale for people who like story rich games.  Here is what you need to know:
+Doing all interactions through the phone is very well done.
+Phone UI includes a menu of sorts that shows options of things to do next, and choices you have made.
+All character personalities and writing is well done, but...
-Some of the in-person acting via video seems weak, but part of it could be the inherent awkwardness of characters or their situations.
-The story doesn't seem to really branch out, as it seems more on rails than branching given that choices influence actions that contribute to the end result but don't have a notable impact on the story other than how characters react/feel about you.
-Your in-game surroundings/background and the rare background noises outside of the phone have no relevance to what is actually going on, other than to set a "mood" and randomly have the chance at jump scaring you.  IMO all jump scares should happen within the context of what is ACTUALLY happening, otherwise the other jump scares have faster diminishing returns.
?I don't know that I was compelled enough by the story to want to play through again at 3-4 hours length to get a different ending and see how they interact with me differently.

review_text_raw:
[h1] The game that was lying around in my steam library that I only played because I had a big Space Engineers update and wanted to kill time [/h1]

See I like the game and had a lot of fun with it, but like most things with a good beginning and middle section, it fell apart at the end and failed to conclude itself well; albeit there are multiple endings, I felt the ending I was given explained nothing, left me with more questions to ask than there were questions answered and left a bad taste in my mouth. Maybe this is the developers way of getting me to play the entirety of the game [spoiler] four [/spoiler] times over to achieve every ending and get the answers I need, but when every playthrough will have the majority of the same content in it every time, it gets a bit boring.

Spoilers below for people that wanna know why I was so dissatisfied with my ending:
[spoiler] So my ending was one of the guys you get close with gets lured into meeting this missing girl and ultimately gets assimilated because of it, the whole idea behind the ending is that I supposedly did not gain this guys trust and therefore he took matters into his own hands, then it turns out that the whole thing was run by some AI with sentience (I'm not too sure if that was the case, but the ending was so just chucked together half of it went over my head (I did try and gain sense of it, I swear!!)). The reason this tilts me so much is that I swear to you I didn't do anything for this guy not to trust me so I was shocked when he starts lashing out about being the sidekick. [/spoiler]

In conclusion:
Great game, awful ending that was chucked together and lacked depth.

review_text_raw:
Note: Posting on my Boyfriend's behalf as he played my copy of it. 

So, let me start off by saying this review's gonna contain MAJOR plot spoilers!  So, only read after you've played it.
Pre-spoiler: The game was good.  Leaves some room for improvement, but overall worth your time, at the very least.

****SPOILER STARTS NOW****



So, I'd say overall, I really did like this game.  The jumpscares are by far the worst part of it, as it's honestly the cheapest form of horror, but the atmosphere was built beautifully.  The actors did a great job making their acting believable.  Greg's actor started off sounding very off, but started getting more and more believable as the game went on.
As for the plot, it's very clearly inspired by stuff like Metal Gear Solid 2.  Though, admittedly it kinda blew the secret open from the very start, with the very first action by the player being to watch a video that kinda gives the twist away, unsubtly at that.  It was very obvious from the moment they started accusing each other that Greg and Taylor were red herrings, so it felt a little forced that I had to investigate both, even if I was given the opportunity to just believe them.
And, that leads me to the endings.  I got the "Abandon All Hope" ending, and haven't experienced the others, nor do I know what happens in them.  Honestly, I like the idea that no one will trust you if you don't trust them, but I'm not a huge fan of the game constantly hammering at me at the very ending that I fucked up.  Though, I do like the touch that the game conditions you early on to investigate everything, thus requiring some thought from the player to not keep doing that for everyone.
One last thing: I see your Telltale inspiration in telling you the major decision points and comparing it to everyone else's.  And, while it's a good way to keep track of what decisions were hard or easy to make, it kinda pulls the curtain away from how shallow the choice system is, basically telling the player all the choices that actually matter, and showing off just how binary they are.  Not saying you need to put hours of depth into literally hundreds of decisions, just saying showing the player a quantifiable chart of choices gives away the whole thing.

Overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth the $5 my boyfriend paid for it, and I can't wait to see more from this developer
