review_text_raw:
The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

Overall, really really impressed. I'll be going back to it for the other endings for sure.

review_text_raw:
Pretty good, truth to be told.

After receiving a mysterious phone, you quickly realize it belongs to a missing young girl, and so you start investigating over her disappearance. Using real life-like apps mimicking twitter, facebook, and Gmail (among others), you'll collect proofs, find connections and chat with the girl's acquaintances to discover an ominous truth.

The ending is a bit of a letdown, but the experience as a whole is engaging.

The game's realization did allow for some immersion and suspension of disbelief and, while there are times where as a player you are pushed in a direction you would not choose, the game flows otherwise quite nicely.

While you are investigating there are some things to do on the side: ominous messages to translate, numbers to use to unlock secret messages, etc. I don't know how many of them are around, but the one I found were a nice diversion.

Acting and voice-acting are also enjoyable most of the time: you have the impression to deal with real people and not actors, usually.

There is not much as far as audio effects are concerned, with the exception of some creepy sound ambiances in superb 3D that did actually made me jump a couple of times.

Also, the game is supposed to be replayable, there are different endings but, frankly after you find out what was all about, I don't see why one should actually do it, unless really really into the game.

All in one a pretty good game, especially for the price.

3.5/5

review_text_raw:
A refreshingly unique concept for a video game. It does involve a lot of reading but it was usually very well written and hence would usually be very interesting. I am not someone who enjoys games that have too much reading but this game is a surprising exception. 
The concept for the game was so interesting but did they execute it well? Yes, a thousand times yes. So glad I purchased this game and so glad I played it. I played the whole thing in one sitting.

Very well written, your decisions do matter as they have consequences. Some of the characters are very likeable as well.  

You feel like a detective uncovering a mysterious and horrifying story. 
Regarding the horror, it doesnt have too much horror honestly - and some of the horror are just jumpscares. However its not all jumpscares. Some of the horror is due to the story and it's twists and revelations, due to its suspense as you figure out things. 

Massive amount of replayability too, it seems to have several endings depending on your choices.

The ending scenes gave me goosebumps and were genuinely terrifying at times. 

Really well done by the developers, shows they put in a massive amount of thought and work into this, very great product and a completely unique experience. A rare gem.

review_text_raw:
It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

review_text_raw: One of my favorite horror games. I'm not generally huge into the genre but the game allows you to do a lot more with your phone than I would've expected, I've probably spent half of my time in the game just fake trolling on the Jabbr app in the game. By far the best part of this game is the sound design, there are plenty of times where you'll hear a noise and it will actually sound like it's coming from the room you're sitting in. It's not the scariest game but the story is fun and engaging the first time through and it's a quick enough play that getting the other endings is quick and easy, plus once you've finished the story one time through it will give you a new game plus option that speeds up all of the text greatly. The voice acting is really cheesy but I found it to be charming, and even though the voice acting is cheesy, most of the text interactions are fairly realistic and very well written. Well worth the low price and a great game for streaming if you like to mess around and do dumb things.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

review_text_raw:
Great idea, but bad execution. A for effort but C on the result.

PROS:
- Technical polish. The UI looks good and the videos, picture and audio are of good quality.
- The developers did seem to put their heart into this. It is not easy to make games involving so much detail, actors and voice work
- Interesting concept. While not original, piercing the story together through different apps on the phone was neat
- Some puzzles were neat like finding a phone number hidden in Twitter posts or creating a specific Tinder profile, because they fit the concept of the game really well

CONS:
- All the characters are downright unlikable.. I didn't care for Anna one bit and if there was an ending to kill them all off I would have took it. And when I mean all, I really mean all. Every single one, including her mother and the HR lady. I guess only the cat gets a pass and even then I'm not sure
- Unrealistic voice work. Most characters speak very unnaturally. The biggest offender being Greg who talks like he is in a kid's anime
- You can only speak to people when they are online, but they always pop up immediately when you need them to make progress, making it very obvious you are playing a videogame. A few seconds delay would have done wonders for the immersion
- Repetitive gameplay. Most of the time you will be doing the same "construct a phrase" or "remake a picture" puzzle and the whole cycle of restoring the phone data should have only happened once.
- Cheap cheap "horror" with zero atmosphere but instead lots of dumb jump-scares (really really a lot) and in-your-face weirdness. No subtlety whatsoever, making the "horror" cheap, pointless and braindead
- The ending. I felt dumber after the villain reveal and finished the game. Not sure I can put up with another run to see the other endings. I was expecting something stupid, but this worse than I expected

They really should have either cut the "horror" and gone full psychological crime thriller (which would have worked really well with the gameplay) or just go full ham and make the weirdness go on through the whole experience escalating more and more.
Instead you get a detective story ruined by awful jump scares or a horror story bogged down by boring detectice work. I would prefer the former as the later was really really bad, inspired by the worst horror movies the '10s had to offer.

I can forgive the bad dialogues and bad acting due to being an indie game, but I would suggest the developers to at least not use outdated memes in people's speech.

Only buy it on sale and expect a mediocre experience that pisses you off because it had the potential to be much better.

Fun little puzzle/"hacking" simulator with creepy supernatural elements. The dialogue is a bit sloppy, and the voice acting is laughably bad, but the storyline is engaging enough for multiple playthroughs. Gameplay is fairly standard for these sorts of games (not a bad thing), and character interactions seem natural enough to maintain immersion.

Don't expect much in the way of a challenge, though; the emphasis is definitely more on the progression of the story and the character interactions. The puzzles (and I'm using the word loosely here) consist of very simple "decrypting" of texts and photos, as well as base-tier social engineering to suss out key bits of information (to be used to unlock accounts, etc). You'll want to keep a notebook and a pen handy, especially if you're trying to collect achievements.

All in all, a fun game that's definitely worth a few bucks and a couple of hours.

review_text_raw:
Honestly a fun little horror game that's worth the price of admission. I'm a sucker for games like this involving fake OS' and learning its quirks and involving myself in this pseudo world of fake apps and this game pulls it off quite well. 

My original run in with this game was watching a twitch streamer named MOONMOON play through it on Halloween back when it first came out and I remember enjoying watching him play through it. So much so that I would rewatch the stream while it was still available in the archives. 

My only gripes with the game are minor and honestly just wanting more things to do. I wanted to explore more of the apps and more websites inside this universe, but kept getting cut off and I would just be like aww okay. I loved the idea of the pseudo Twitter named "Jabbr" and how you can just openly respond to people. What I would've loved more is if the people actually responded to you in some form or fashion, even if its just some default responses, its better than just no one ever saying anything. 

My only other negative I would say is [spoiler] the villain or the Simulacra as you can call it is honestly a bit goofy. The idea of him is interesting but his ramblings and ideology as he just sits there and spews it to you sounds like someone who thinks their better than everyone ramble on about what perfect utopia they want. It just comes off as whiny and a bit silly. Also, during repeat runs, its a bit annoying that I can't skip its dialogue at all. It gets annoying listening to him say the same things over and over and I wish I could fast text through it like you can with the text messages themselves in NG+ [/spoiler]

Took me a while to finally sit and play it myself and I'm glad I did. Even though I knew what was going to happen, I still thoroughly enjoyed my time with it and I'm very excited to see what the sequel adds to it.

review_text_raw:
This is a tough call, especially given the price of the game. I'm going negative here because the "Overwhelmingly Positive" is out of line. This game is average, at best.

The concept itself is unique and the gameplay, for the most part, is well developed.

The main problem is the /r/nosleep storyline and unprofessional voice actors (especially Greg, I actually physically cringed when listening to his line deliveries). On top of that, there's some laughably blunt social commentary that's simply ridiculous. Someone else said it well, if they were going to be camp, they should have just gone all out campy horror. review_text_raw:
[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience. To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life. The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal. There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. This game wasn't my bag.

review_text_raw:
Yooooo this game is cool!  Simulacra is my first Kaigan game, so if it cribs from any other games they've made, I wouldn't know yet (I've seen reviews saying this game is similar to others, but I'm fresh to the series/catalog..)  

In my first play-through, I failed hard.. Without spoiling too much, let it suffice to say I didn't save the people I was supposed to save.

Some positives:  The choices in the game actually have some bearing on the outcome of the game.  In my first play-through, I chose to be snarky/sarcastic at times.  My snark made me laugh at the time, but came back to bite me in the end.

I find myself _wanting_ to play again, so I can make better decisions.

Some slight negatives: The acting is a wee bit corny at times, but overall, mostly well-done.  Also, the conversation feels a bit "forced" sometimes.  That happens with games like this -- basically, sometimes, it feels like, no matter what you say, the response you get is the same..  I understand that that's a consequence of having to wrap dialog up, but sometimes the progression can be jarring.  Still, it's only a minor issue. 

To me, this game is not very scary (but I have a pretty high horror threshold, so take what I say with a grain of salt.. I watched the original "It" when I was 7 years old.. then I leaned into the whole horror movie/horror game thing..  I watch horror movies alone, in the dark.. So.. yeah..)

Still, overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game.  I found the presentation (playing the entire game via the interface of someone else's phone) to be interesting, and I want to play again and figure out how to get more positive endings than the one I got the first time around.

Imagine yourself waking up one day and someone delivered a phone to you, and not any normal phone, it is a missing person's phone. The game starts off with you having Anna's phone, you played a video of her saying weird stuff and not to find her, however, when you go through her messages and dig deeper into her personal life, you will discover many things. Would you trust her boyfriend who seems to be worried or someone who she chatted with online? You will make this choice and end up with one of the four possible endings of this game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997884297

The gameplay is all about texting, reading text messages, going to social media, solve some puzzles to find phone numbers, passwords or people to contact. It is a fun deep game and has lots of jumpscares! I gasped so many times and couldn't stop playing the game until I've finished it, and yes, that took me 9 hours to finish with little breaks in between. 

I was torn between the answers, yes you are limited with the answers they provided you but sometimes you wish to side with someone, the next moment you hear something from the other character which will make you suspect the first one. I ended up suspecting everyone including myself. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997329266

The actors were mediocre, none of them showed the supposed emotion the person would in such a situation, the facial expression wasn't the best especially Anna and Taylor. However the writing of the game and how the story flows is really good, I didn't expect that twist.

After the success of [b]Sara Is Missing[/b], it was obvious [i]Kaigan Games[/i] would continue in the same vein of development. Truth is, before [b]Sara is Missing[/b], there was [b]Finding Home[/b], an indie game also simulating a smartphone experience. Seems the studio entire direction is surrounded by this peculiar genre, one that connects players into a stylized voyeur adventure never seen before.

In [b]SIMULACRA[/b] players gain access to a smartphone belonging to a young woman named Anna. She’s just like any other girl in her early 20’s, working and having a good time with her friends online and offline. All seems perfectly fine, except Anna went missing and she left a strange, bizarre video, as her last registered action.

The overall story is embedded within Anna’s online actions, and each new lead will reveal parts of her past, with phone backups and confessions from her friends. Dialogues are pretty realistic and interesting, making the overall experience more pleasant. There’s no drama, but it’s still somehow intense with a touch of horror and matching jump scares.

Players will explore Anna’s inner secrets and sneak peek into her life, as well as in her problems. Through smartphone apps, such as email, chats, and even the equivalent of Twitter and Tinder, we’ll meet her acquaintances and find clues that may lead to Anna’s whereabouts. While browsing text and pictures, we can restore them by either forming a phrase out of loose words, and building an image by restoring little pieces at a time.

Finding Anna is as much part of the story, as create a connection with other persons of interest through social media. You’ll have to find clues and discover ways to connect with others, to collect new information. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] allows you to open up, or, in some cases, keep pretending to be Anna, which may open up new dialogue options and information.

There’s a certain acquired taste when going through someone else’s life, and the game clearly explores that with decency, but still waving a round or two of peculiar situations and encounters. Some internet references and expressions can be found all over the place, adding a certain style and characterization of realism into that social media life.

It’s one of those experiences, where you’ll forget you’re in the game. As soon as the clues start rolling down and the story involving, it’s a fantastic journey. Gathering clues and finding the direction to go was always relatively easy, and I never found myself stuck or without an idea of where to go. The game also contains a section with the objectives, which will help out in most scenarios if needed.

The visual presentation is accurate and suiting. It’s far more comfortable browsing this virtual phone, then rather use a phone in real life obviously, since the game grants resolutions up to your own. Videos and pictures follow the expected quality and it’s an authentic experience as far as design goes.

Indie games featuring live-action performances with quality are rare. Most of the times the studio goes to an alternative or stylized acting. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] though, doesn’t need any of those tricks, and [url=www.instagram.com/wendyvanhoren/]Wendy Van Horen[/url] plays Anna surprisingly well. Some may claim it’s an amateurish act, but remember, this is Anna’s life, a young person sharing vlogs about her personal life experiences. Wendy definitely brings the character alive, adding a natural and realistic touch.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] dwells between our presence in the real world, versus our digital personas. I personally think it’s a really good concept and it’s well depict. Doesn’t become far-fetched, even when dealing with the supernatural. It’s a horror experience, but more towards what social media means to us, and how scary it can become. Very entertaining and for the simple price of $3,99 it’s impossible to avoid recommending this one.

review_text_raw:
As I write this I'm not sure whether or not I will be recommending it or not... I certainly appreciate it for doing something new, and on that level I recommend playing it just so that original ideas get more light brought onto them in a gaming market saturated by copy and pastes of the same MMO or the same First Person Shooter or the same RPG with unnecessary level up mechanics.

That being said, I think it forgets that the game is inherently creepy without needing to throw jumpscares at you. Every time a jumpscare happened I burst into laughter and any amount of tension that had built up was now vanished. Because when it happens, you've been given a signal that now things are going back to normal. The suspense is suddenly lost as you go back to goofing around on someone else's phone.

The game is best described as a cross between Her Story and Orwell but without coming together as nicely as either. I thought that the ending was great, but the path to get there felt a bit too linear. I had figured out how I could get information and obtained information, and then was stuck in a text conversation about how I was going to obtain said information. The freedom in exploration that I was given didn't match some of the conversations that needed to happen. Though there was one bit that was quite nice in that you could figure something out incredibly early without it feeling like you were being roadblocked until another conversation happened.

All in all it's definitely worth checking out, but Her Story and Orwell did it better.

Just finished my first playthrough of this game are here are my thoughts:

Pros:
*Length was good for the price
*Story kept me invested throughout
*Some truly creepy moments that made me think about how themes in the game relate to potential problems in the real world
*A few not-so-obvious puzzles that gave me a sense of satisfaction when I figured them out

Cons:
*Most of the puzzles are pretty weak and repetitive
*There were a couple times where I was having two different conversations with the same person at the same time in the same text thread. I would say this is a glitch thought should have been remedied by now.
*Game crashed three times on me, and my system is no slouch
*The acting is pretty cringe-worthy.
*Ending was pretty unsatisfying, but I can go back and try again I guess...

In the end I think it was definitely worth a couple bucks and was a refreshing departure from the usual.

review_text_raw:
[disclosure: I got this game for $1 as part of a Humble Bundle. I do think it's worth regular price though.]  

I enjoyed the story and felt they made good use of the mobile interface. It's basically a visual novel, so the story's on rails most of the time. However, there are points where your choices affect your relationships with the other characters, or where you know what to do (get in touch with someone) but not how to do it (you don't know her), so you need to get creative. 

Another nice thing about the game itself is the Begin+ feature, which speeds up the dialogue boxes on subsequent playthroughs. That'll get you through the game in about an hour instead of the usual three or four, making it a bit easier to try other paths and find all of the endings (I'm not there yet.) 

On the downside, I could have done without the pop scares. That's about as cheap as horror gets. Also, since the story and its dialogue options are all laid out for you, sometimes I had to say things I didn't believe or reveal information I wouldn't have revealed, and that hurts the immersion for me. Still, these are minor flaws in a fun, quick, entertaining game.

review_text_raw:
8/10 Very Good:


So, think Orwell (if you’ve played that) and you’re sort of on the right track with this one.

It’s a game entirely contained within a fake iPhone. Not even yours. Basically, some girl called Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you start being a real sneaky person and looking into her phone, pictures, e-mail, Twitter and all that.

It transpires, Anna is missing, as in, genuinely a missing person. All you have to go on is a video of her in a state talking about unknown forces and asking that you don't find her. You get sucked into using her phone to investigate where she could be, and ultimately what eventually happened to her. You end up meeting some of her friends and acquaintances via the phone, teaming up as you all strive to find out what has happened to Anna.

It is Live-Action acting as well, some of it is hilariously cringe (in a good, light-hearted way), and the acting isn’t top notch, but… The investigative hook, the story and the conversations within are very good. In fact, you can join in on text conversations, picking from a list of (limited) options to reply to people as you work together to find the truth.

There’s a lot of B-movie tech horror in here as well, it’s designed to be played with headphones and preferably, the lights are off! Expect lots of static, distorted voices and a low horror tone. For me, it was interesting stuff, I had a blast with it, even if I got a pretty bad ending (there are four I think).

Look, this game goes on sale for like £2. There’s no losing with his one, I think it is a very good effort by the developers to make something different and interesting, and more importantly, I think this one kind of works. Check this one out.

The voice acting is terrible and feels very performative, rather than being believable phone calls/voice messages. The story is linear, and there isn't much room for creativity (e.g. sending people random pictures to see how they respond), and there aren't really any things to mess around with on the phone that are interesting. The puzzles are ridiculously simple and serve no purpose other than to slow down the narrative. The jump scares, if you consider them that, are pretty pointless and don't enhance the story or experience whatsoever. The writing is generally bad and unbelievable (e.g. [spoiler]the CEO of Phresh Ideas divulging way too much information [/spoiler]), and many of the dialog options do not make sense at all. The characters frequently go between texting and calling in a way that doesn't feel believable, and behave very strangely (e.g. [spoiler]at the end of the game, a character is literally texting you as he's pushing someone to their death off of a balcony [/spoiler]). After finishing the game you can go back through more quickly to see the alternate endings, but it still takes too long, and you still have to sit through a lot of dialogue at the end at the normal speed.

Ultimately I would not recommend purchasing this game, solely because the primary focus of this game is the narrative and it felt weak. I received this game from a bundle.

review_text_raw:
What's in a phone? As our communications devices draw ever-nearer ourselves, so we begin to be reflected in them. Images, videos, messages, applications, and even layout all vomit a virtual breadcrumb trail that hint at who the owner is.

This is a "found-phone" story. Where is Anna? Who is Anna? What's happening? 

You'll be well-aware of what's happening a few seconds into the game, but the journey is worth it. Additionally, the audio engine ... oh man. I had to stop playing a few times, take off my headphones, and see who was at the door. The audio and spatial-positioning of the audio is very very good.

Edit: just 100% completed this game after playing for 13 hours. Well-worth the list price; I'd buy this again for the experience.

Wow… just wow. This game is really really really good. I didn’t expect it to be that good! 

Honestly, I don’t play much games of this genre. The first one was “Her story”. And this one is similar but waaaaay better.

You found the phone of Ana and need to message her contacts in various apps and use hints in chats and websites to find out what happened to her (she disappeared). 

The riddles are great (I especially enjoyed the one where I had to find cassie’s phone number), the smartphone control is smooth and realistic, the chats are interesting and humorous, and the story was compelling.

It made me want to play Simulacra 2. I must buy it now… But before playing the second one: As I enjoyed Simulacra so much and because I know that there are various endings, I will have to replay this game at least once to take different decisions.

review_text_raw:
For full transparency: I got this game in a Humble bundle worth 0.99 cents along with 1 other game.

[b][u]The good[/u][/b]
This game has an engaging story, I was seriously invested in the characters and how this was gonna play out. The characters really had a personality to them. The performance of the person playing Anna in particular was great! 
I liked the piecing together aspect this game had and how you slowly uncover more. It managed to hold my attention, for sure. It took me on a ride that I really enjoyed.
You can see that there was a lot of time and effort put into this game, with all the different things that are on the phone and all the conversations that play out. The little image and word puzzles were a nice touch, too. The game looks good and for the most part sounds good, too. 


[b][u]The bad[/u][/b]
The big reveal at the end of the game was… meh. The mystery to the game was much more fun than the answer to that mystery. Although I did like the endings themselves and their ambiguity.  
There were some repeated grammar mistakes that took me out of the experience. Yes, it’s texting, but I feel like in texting you get more typos and less grammar mistakes. The game would benefit from fixing some of these.
The voice acting was a bit spotty. Some actors did a good job, like the detective or Taylor. However, there was one audio clip of Ashley that felt immersion-breaking to me, and Greg in general didn’t sound good to me at all, it was way over the top.

[b]I encountered a game-breaking bug.[/b] For some reason, if you go in the web browser and go to the history section, all web pages that you should only be supposed to look at later in the game are already available. If you read these, events will trigger and the game will think you’re already at those points. The game then runs both the conversations you were already having and the “new” conversations which completely breaks your savefile. So, until this bug is fixed, [b]don’t look at anything in the history section of the web browser[/b].

[b]TL;DR Nice game, I definitely recommend it! But beware of the bug I talked about ^[/b]

Aside from that, it's a pretty solid indie product, it looks really polished and it performs well on my PC. I think maybe that's why the poor spelling stands out so much. Still, worth getting on sale and playing for a couple hours - though I would recommend that you [b][i]NOT[/i][/b] play this in one sitting: you will get annoyed and sick of this game, it is best enjoyed in short bursts.

I am late as hell but wow, I gotta say it doesn't matter what time you decide to play this game.  If you like Psychological Horror games then this is one to check out.  It's dirt cheap at only 5 bucks (2.24) at the time of this review.  I have always been a fan of investigation games and this one is unique in it's delivery.  Putting you in control of a missing girl's phone to slowly uncover what happened or what is happening to her is one of the best experiences I have had in a while.  This game records your choices and all of them affect the outcome of the ending you get.  There are multiple endings so don't just stop at one play through.  It even tells you what percent of the players made the same decisions that you did, similar to how games like Telltale's The Walking Dead or Life Is Strange do it.  If you are a fan of detective games and psychological horror games.  You owe it to yourself to at least try Simulacra.  My first play through took me about 3.6 hours and that was me trying to do just about everything.  I am definitely going to be going at it again to see the other endings

review_text_raw:
If you like eerie, cerebral horror, I highly recommend Simulacra, especially in a bundle with its sequel.  Things you get: 
* A new kind of evil
* Choices that matter (multiple endings)
* A very believable phone to snoop through.   The photos and other clues all blend extremely well with what you'd expect out of a typical phone. 
* Puzzles to solve, with clues often embedded into the content in ways that are not painfully obvious
* Identity theft for a good cause. 
* Both likable and unlikable characters

The only downsides here are that some of the acting quality is kind of meh, but it's an indie game, Play at night with the lights off.  This is a suspense-thriller, not a jumpscare horror-fest, so while there are a few "gotcha" moments, it is the subtle creepy stuff that will get to you.  Best played without "scouting" the plot online first; the villain reveal is much more interesting this way. 

There is also a Free to Play demisequel called Simulacra: Pipe Dreams, so if you're going for the complete collection, you need this, Simulacra 2, and Pipe Dreams.

review_text_raw:
A decent puzzle type game. While there are the occasional mild jump scares and something strange going on, it didn't really give me a horror or suspense vibe.

Pros:
- I generally stay away from FMV games, but the actresses & voice actors are actually pretty good
- The puzzle difficulty is OK for the most part
- Several other easter eggs and hidden puzzles if you want an extra challenge
- Has a mode for replaying to make text speed up instead of being at a realistic speed

Cons:
- Lacking in horror, and didn't feel that suspenseful
- Texts and responses when texting are often not quite right - grammatically wrong or just don't completely make sense. It could have used some more polish.
- Setting aside the fact that you're going through a stranger's phone instead of giving it to the police/family/etc, there are still things you have to do to progress the story that I would never think to do IRL
- While you frequently have different options for responses to messages, responses to what you say are frequently reused, giving the illusion of more choice than you really have. Good for role playing, but noticeable when replaying
- Has mutually exclusive achievements and different endings, but lacks replayability. Yes you can choose different dialogue option that can influence people differently, but the puzzles and their solutions are still the same.
- I wasn't a big fan of the ending. It didn't make much sense and wasn't really explained. That may have been saved for the second game though.

Verdict: 7/10

I've never played a game quite like this before, and for that alone I will recommend it. You basically have the phone of a missing girl and attempt to rescue/find out what happened to her by snooping through her phone. You slowly get access to more and more features of her phone (sometimes in really clever ways, like figuring out her password to an app). Slowly a horror plot unfolds as you find out more and more about what happened.

The acting in the game... is pretty amateurish. Plus there are a few far fetched events that take place. But overall the story is compelling enough, and the gimmick of the entire game being played as going through someones phone well done enough, that you still get sucked in.

There are multiple endings, and to get the best endings (as is usually the case) you will have to play through multiple times to see everything. Luckily the speed things up for your second+ playthroughs. Also the horror never really gets too scary, but it does get a bit creepy at times.

Overall definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys video games that push the medium a little.

review_text_raw:
I am generally biased to be forgiving of FMV interactive movies, so of course I've played others like Her Story, #WarGames, The Bunker, Late Shift, and The Shapeshifting Detective.  Like those games, this game is relatively short on total content, with moments of good acting and then...well, near-miss moments that make you cringe.  Also, these games tend to have multiple achievements and scenes that you can't get in one playthrough, which is a way of extending the replay value, but I seldom feel particularly inclined to watch the repeated parts over and over again.

This game is unique due to the phone interface and the clever design that it took to make that work.  You feel like it really could be you deciding what to do in this situation, but then sometimes you're reminded how you can't actually do anything like answer a phone call.  So when it works, it's great, but it has built-in limitations to just how far the concept can go.  I commend them for the creepy story.  I wish the really uneven voice acting hadn't pulled me out of it from time to time.  At least Anna (whose phone you've found) is done consistently well.

Your first full playthrough will take 3-4 hours depending on how much you read, and subsequent plays should take you a bit less.  Alternate achievements, videos, conversations, and endings are basically earned by the responses you choose, like who to be nice to, who to scold, and who to trust.  The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths.  In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story.  But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find.  So you know what you're getting.  If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

review_text_raw:
Summary: For a horror/mystery/puzzle game, it is quite weak on each of the three elements. The least surprising mystery game I've played. Perhaps mainly because it blows its load from the start and spends the rest of the play time catching up with itself. Probably works better on mobile, as it seems made for a short attention span.

Pros:
- Basic concept is a cool commentary on social media and online dating
- A couple of surprising moments
- Some easter eggs and alternative paths give a bit of replay value

Cons:
- Storytelling is overstated and predictable
- Dialog is unconvincing, and I often didn't like my choices
- Game is linear and holds your hand almost the entire way. Some light puzzles, but otherwise no challenge, except unlocking a certain ending
- Acting is meh, supporting voice acting is mostly plain bad
- Annoying spelling errors are not always intentional

For examples of similar storytelling that really works: see Oxenfree and Doki Doki Literature Club.

Mostly liked this game.

There were a few good varied 'puzzles' for finding passwords etc, which I liked.

The storyline and dialogue was written so that i was never entirely sure who kidnapped the phone's owner.

On conclusion of the game, it was interesting to see what choices affected the outcome, and used that to try for alt. endings.
After the first completion, the game runs quicker on replay, tho wd have preferred ability to click thru the dialogues instead.
As there are no save points, there is no option but to replay the whole thing for alt. endings and achievements.
It was quicker the second time, due to knowing which files arent necessary to activate or find clues in.

Besides no skip scene options, the gameplay was intuitve and the production was good.
My only peeve was one of the characters. Tho he is supposed to be and ass, and i did get him to apologise to me, on the second run-thru (probably coz i had less patience for his bs) he rrreeealllly iritated me. Being an important character, there is no avoiding him and i just wanted to smack him in the head. So many times I wanted to just 'hang up' on him, tho there isnt that ability, and found myself actually talking back to him, in frustration of what a dick he is. If you like these 'Missing Phone Owner' games, and can tolerate a doosh, you will like this game.

review_text_raw:
Went into this completely blind and found it to be a decent game with a slightly above average horror storyline. There are a lot of jump-scare tactics in this visual novel/detective game, many of them unnecessary and overused. The FMVs were done pretty well and the interface is intuitive. The game encourages you to play it again to get different outcomes, but when the first playthrough is over 3 hours I can't be bothered to play a linear story and make sure that I selected certain dialogue options to get all endings/100% achievements.

One thing that I absolutely found hilarious was Greg's voice acting. It's so campy and over-the-top that the first time I heard it I couldn't help but bust out laughing. I'm sure that when he recorded it he had to be clear and precise with his lines, but holy crap it just sounds like a Dragonball Z character powering up for a fight.

I recommend this only because what it does well, it does it *really* well (atmosphere, NPC dialogue, FMV, interface). For the other stuff, it's borderline 80's slasher B-movie status trying to take itself a bit too seriously. There seemed to be some missed opportunities here and gaping plot holes, but I would play another game very similar to this by the same developer with a few new tricks.

Overall, mostly worth your time. Might play Simulacra 2 when I get the chance.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Final Verdict: Buy! Spoiler-Free Review.[/h1]

This game took me about 3.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (there are alternate endings available). I tried to read every bit of text and watch every video / photo involved. This game does disappoint as a horror game, but as a mystery thriller, it is excellent. 

This is not a mixed or alternate reality game where you search the web for answers or give your e-mail. The experience is pretty linear, although you can make different choices, the experience goes pretty much through the same set of main events (except for the endings which can vary). You will be looking through videos, photos, Jabbr (facebook), Spark (Tinder), the web (in-game only browser), phone numbers, and e-mails. You simply have to find the relevant information to unlock passcodes or find connections to progress the story. 

You will also have dialogue choices. Some of those choices can have an impact on the story, for example, having more trust with that person and thus giving you a different ending. The story starts out very strong when it is a mystery about what happened to the missing woman, Anna. Even the creepy stuff is exciting at first when you see the distorted videos and the atmosphere leaves things to the imagination. The dialogue between characters is well-written. 

Unfortunately, when you find out the mystery then the horror elements become more silly than scary. I actually just started to troll everybody, trying to get the worst possible ending. There was some real tension at the start and middle of this game, but towards the end, I really didn't feel any connection to any of the characters or "the danger" involved.

That's a shame because this is a very polished experience. The actors all did a nice job overall (sure some of the acting could have been better, but it's better than what is in most games). The mystery sequences where you're sleuthing and trying to find the truth all work extremely well. It's just too bad it ends in a whimper instead of a bang.

[b]Rate 7/10. I still recommend this. With a better ending(s), this could have been something very special. Good overall, but should have been great![/b]

TLDR: Cute little horror game with lots of jump scares and some bad acting. Social media in this game was amazing fun. Pick it up on sale.

An adventure horror game all happening in somebody's phone. You essentially play as yourself, trying to solve the mystery of the phone's owner's disappearance with the help of her friends. The puzzles are not very difficult, but engaging enough to keep you hooked in the story. There were some really spooky segments so I'd recommend playing this in a dark quiet room to get its full potential.

The story was fun, reasonably short. Editing Anna's social media was definitely the biggest highlight of my playthrough - you get absolute freedom in Anna's phone. Devs could only make this better by adding more consequences to it. You will spend a lot of time talking to 2 of the biggest cringelords in games everywhere. Their strange behavior was topped off by their atrocious acting. Female acting was alright. There are multiple endings to reflect your choices.

All in all, I recommend getting this one on sale. It's not the best or most memorable game ever, but it's still fairly entertaining..

review_text_raw:
[b]SIMULACRA[/b] is detective visual novel with a hint of horror and a unique presentation and a couple of simple puzzles. The whole story unfolds on the screen of a phone lost by a missing girl. You start by looking through her videos, photos and chat history. There are even some interesting puzzles where you have to answer personal questions to restore password. But then the game shifts to the classic visual novel style, which uses chat windows instead of dialogue boxes. It becomes boring and the dialogue writing is kind of bad, expect stupid jokes and useless sentences. Another thing that made my walkthrough impossible are jumpscares, why put them in a game where you have to focus to read text? Somebody's gonna have a heart attack from this.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Unique presentation
+ Interesting 30-60 minutes of gameplay in the beginning

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Jumpscares
- Boring dialogue that tries too much to be funny
- Not much in terms of gameplay

The game has a great concept, looking through personal stuff to figure out what happened is interesting, but the game ditches it in less than an hour. If you were interested in the game because of it, you should try [b]Telling Lies[/b], which explores this same idea, but sticks to it for the whole game.

review_text_raw:
In Simulacra you find yourself in possession of a stranger's (Anna) phone, who seems to have come to some harm. Through interactions with her phone via video logs, old chat messages, pictures, etc, you gain access to Anna's backstory. Going forward, primarily through "live" chats with Anna's acquaintances, and interactions with some of the other apps on the phone, you unravel the story.

Pros:
[list]
[*] The story progression as implemented through the interactions with the phone apps is OK.
[*] The real-life acting done by Anna and Taylor was good.
[*] The concept of this experience was novel (at least to me).
[/list]

YMMV:
[list]
[*] There are different endings possible, as a function of your choices. I typically don't like this choose-your-adventure type of feature, as it turns into a "guess what the dev" wants me to say sort of thing. Also, this game is nowhere near interesting enough to warrant a second play through, so you are stuck with whatever ending your seemingly random choices yield. For me, this was the "bad" (maybe even super bad?) ending, which left a bad taste in my mouth, and made me feel as though I had wasted my time.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*] The two oft repeated mini-games aren't really fun, and seem shoe-horned in, in an effort to somehow make this more into a game. It doesn't really work. I would classify this as an "experience" more than a "game".
[*] The story itself was underwhelming. 
[/list]

Conclusion: Read the reviews carefully before purchasing this one and get it on sale. It may be a mildly amusing way to pass several hours, but it certainly isn't for everyone. Giving a weak-thumbs up due to binary rating system.

Overall: 5.0/10

It's not super time consuming: I finished it in two and a half hours the first time, though I did watch a youtuber playthrough so I knew a bit, and once I had begin+ to speed up chat and knew what to do, it took me an hour. Overall, definitely a worthwhile purchase.

review_text_raw:
The game has potential with its premise.
However, it handles it so, so poorly.
Tried all the endings and variation of the game.

The interface is crisp and the chat messages actually pretty good. Going through messages, characters are both flawed and likeable and the writing does text messaging very well, it doesn't feel too cringe nor too forced.

The thing is, going through someone's messages and all that already does what the game wants; think about what you're doing with someone's privacy. However, by the end of it, it will rub its "simulacra" psychological message in your face in the edgiest, most infantile way. I get it, its a black mirror, its such a smart and deep(TM) plot you have.

But the worst part of the game is the acting.
Upon playing, you will see a set of videos and some people (aka one character) will send you video messages. The thing is.
THE. ACTING. IS. MONSTROUSLY. CRINGE.
It is very, very, VERY bad acting. Not in the way that sometimes in a small game, you'll see a dev do a few lines and it feels a bit awkward, but it's serviceable. No. I have no idea who the actors are, but they feel like very, VERY bad amateur actors trying way too hard to be good actors, but also act like they think they are very good actors. One of the character is supposed to be to some extent a cringy kind of person, but it is not the character that is cringe, the way the actor playing the character is really cringe. I have no idea who the actors are, but it genuinely feel like the it's the dev who just hired his girl crush being like "You have a cute face you're gonna be a star in my game". It is just that tryhard cringy.

Now you think "Oh its a phone game so you'll mostly see text messaging". No, by the time you reach the second half, you'll be bombarded with video and they will be all as painful to watch as the next one. Which is a goddamn shame, because during my playthrough, the messaging back and forth with those characters felt good and compelling.

If you're curious about the game, really, just watch a playthrough online.

review_text_raw:
Playable, but not to my tastes.

Simulacra is a simple investigative game that requires patience not for the investigation itself, but for its unnatural writing (very clearly non-native English) and its amateurish acted scenes. Jokes dropped like lead balloons, tension dissipated, and what should have been an exciting climax was simply uncomfortable.

The puzzles themselves were relatively entertaining - flicking between apps to piece together information - but the game's "OS" seemed almost incapable of multitasking, and switching between tabs would typically lose form entry data, making the process far more tedious than it should have been.

The game encourages the player to play through multiple times (with a fast-dialogue option after completion), but one playthrough felt like a slog, so I'm unlikely to sit through it again. If you happen to have it in your Steam library, give it a shot, but don't get your hopes too high.

review_text_raw:
You might think that this is a real-life mystery-horror thriller but no, you will find out that it is a B film in disguise - nonsensical plot, cringy acting, annoying jumpscares, and clichéd ending in one package!

The game was quite intriguing in the beginning. We have to use someone's phone to find out what happened to its owner. To my disappointment, the game got downhill fast.

Puzzles were OK, but watching the video messages was painful. If the devs didn't have enough fundings to hire good actors, then why not just leave out the video? They don't contribute to the plot anyway. There were also jumpscares, which were so out of place and annoying, all sense of immersion I had was ruined by them.

[spoiler]The worst was the ending. The villain was revealed to be an AI called Simulacra, who wanted to kill Anna because, in Simulacra's own words, she "is a worm in a perfect image that needs to be eradicated". Was this line supposed to be scary? Why does Simulacra speak like a cartoon villain?

The ending left me with more questions than answers. The biggest question is: How does an entity that only exists in the virtual space hijack people's bodies in real life?!?!?! Is there a Wi-Fi receiver in the human brain!? 

Even the story premise falls apart when you think about it: 
WHY did the villain/sockpuppet leave the phone on the player's doorstep in the first place?
If Simulacra could imitate other people in the cyberspace, then it could have just destroyed the phone and used Anna's identity to lure more victims online (indeed, at one point in the game Simulacra successfully wiped the phone data), instead of letting the player find out about Anna, who might then rescue her, or worse, warn everyone in the world about the existence of a cyberspace killer. On the topic of warning people, why didn't people who knew Anna contact the police instead of trying to solve the case on their own? When even an ordinary person realised that something fishy was going on, how come the police knew nothing about the disappearances when all the missing people had interacted with each other before they went missing? Did they not bother to do basic investigations?[/spoiler]

Finally, as a VN, being unable to manually save is unacceptable. You have to replay the game from the beginning to get an alternative ending.

It's a shame as this game had great potential to educate people about phone addiction and danger of social media.

review_text_raw:
Now this is how you do a smartphone mystery right. The concept of Sara is Missing was sound, but the execution was poor. However, Kaigan Games took the concept and criticism, and further developed the core concept further in Simulacra. 

Simulacra does a fantastic job in making you the player feel lost and isolated. You are in a dimly lit room with constant noises around you - you are never allowed to feel comfortable where you are, or with what you are doing. You have a random woman's phone, and it is up to you to find her. You have to dig through her e-mails, Jabber and Spark accounts, and decide which of her friends and acquaintances can be trusted with crucial information related to Anna's disappearance.

The tension is real. Should you really be doing this? Wouldn't it be easier to just contact the police? But can the police even find her with so little information? Which of her friends can be trusted? Could one of them be responsible for her disappearance?  The whole time something feels off from the very beginning. Are you being watched? 

The only real gripe I have with the game is the jump scares. Jump scares are for cheap low-level horror titles. And I don't necessarily mean cheap in terms of dollar value - a lot of AAA titles misuse jump scares and it's pathetic. One or two carefully placed jump scares in appropriate games is fine, but Simulacra isn't one of them. The fear comes from the tension and subtle little nuances. When the phone goes crazy and suddenly the picture of Anna on the wallpaper changes slightly, but you're not sure if you imagined it or not - perfect. Loud noises and jumbled up pictures - stupid. 

All-in-all Simulacra is a terrific experience if you like these kind of horror games. Don't let Sara is Missing deter you from trying out Kaigan Games other titles, unlike a lot of other developers, they took the criticisms they received and learned from them to craft better experiences. That alone makes this game worth checking out.

Well for a "Phone Simulator" it aint a bad game. Actually I enjoyed the story a lot but there were also a couple things I didnt like.

[spoiler]The first and only timed event is a bit harsh...theres a lot of talking that you needa read before you can actually react. When you finally have control over what happens they ask you to input things that you are not familiar with at this point of the story. Yes you can know them but youre not that far into it at this point to "know" them to enter those words within 30 seconds.
Another point I didnt like is that sometimes your choice really isnt clear enough. I knew exactly what I would do in specific situations and Im presented with choices that I cant really make sense of. Sometimes the outcome went into a different direction than I intended.
Last points are about the ending. Of course I got an ending I didnt like. I saved one and sacrificed another. Im not clear as to what the entity was referring with if things went differently I could have changed its mind and Im not playing through  this again to find out. Also during the last conversations I unlocked a vlog entry and got a couple chat messages...I was unable to actually read or view them since the final conversation...well youre locked in it.[/spoiler]

Technically I had three problems with it. First when I started it I got a black screen. Im running Win10 and had to run it in Win7 compatibility mode with fullscreen optimizations disabled. Than I had no sound because for some reason it automatically switched to my turned off headset. After fixing that I could play the whole game without problems. After the credits it went to black screen again so i hadt to alt+f4 it.

Anyway...story is great if you like to read...if you like adventures with not too hard riddles...go for it...the price is cheap for the hours of entertainment that you get.

Got this via Humble ... but I gotta say, ugh, phff, well, no.

Maybe someone can find this interesting, but to me I just played it out of curiosity to see what it's about. And it only took 3 hours for 1 playthrough.

Gameplay is minimal. You "chat" with people mostly and sometimes you gotta play a bit of detective, but, nah.

I guess it might have been more interesting if the story had actually been good, if the characters had been likeable, but they're all very annoying people, even Ashley. Seriously, this game does not have a single human being ... or maybe it IS close to real and that would be even more depressing.

Using the apps was tedious, switching between apps meant progress was mostly lost, which slows down progress. Some hints are so "obscure" that you will have forgotten all about them when you actually need them halfway through the game. Some things are illogical.

The dialogue could carry such a game, but it's not well-written (and they do not speak EN as their mother tongue). It's cringy, annoying, irritating, endless (seriously, just write out the text in 1 message, not 10).

In any case the story makes little sense. Spoiler: It's not a thriller, it's "supernatural". That is made clear from the very beginning, but not on the store page. I expected an actual crime, not some pseudo horror trip with bad "explanations".

Honestly, I just wanted to tell the guys to leave me the fuck alone. I'll try out the 2nd game as well to see what they changed, but I do hope there's a "fuck you all" button.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interactive horror movie displayed through an emulated mobile phone screen.  You've got someone else's phone and for some reason you're texting her boyfriend and watching spooky videos because something went wrong.  Spooky technology glitches! oooOOOoooo. 

I think FMV can be an excellent tool in storytelling and video game creation if used right.  Looking at games that worked, like Press X Not To Die and Mortal Kombat, you can see why.  Simulacra isn't one of the ones that works.  The story is below Blair Witch 4 kind of stuff, it's not gripping.  The bits where you're texting other people is badly written.  I understand the developers wanted to emulate a mobile phone, but looking at my 4K monitor being wasted displaying a 9:16 aspect ratio is just depressing.

There's better ways to tell a story than we can see in Simulacra.  For less money than they're asking for this you could rent any schlock horror film online and have a far better time, with better writing and acting, too.  If you did end up with this in the Humble Bundle and accidentally launched it, be aware the game crashes when you try to exit, and you have to go find the rogue process and kill it.

This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones. 

If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:

https://youtu.be/KQoCrsCpfF0
