review_text_raw:
Simulacra is essentially a found footage film but as a game.
One day someone leaves you a phone at your doorstep, which belongs to a girl that has gone missing.
From there, it's your job to snoop through her phone to uncover hints on what happened to her.
The actors can be very cheesy and hardly believable, but that has it's own charm if you are into that kind of thing. The problem I had with the story was the horror elements that they try to shove in, in the form of jump scares. Apart from being the annoying type of jump scares, they also immediately take the story in a direction, where you as the player know where the story will end up. If the jump scares where replaced with more subtle hints that something is off, I think it would have been a lot more engaging.
  
To give credit to the devs, they did a good job at imitating a phone OS with  multiple apps. That makes it fun to snoop around for clues on how to gain access to specific parts of the phone. Even though you have a variety of apps to explore, however, multitasking is something that the fake OS lacks, which makes jumping back and forth from different apps a chore. Having to constantly scroll through everything to get to the part you need can quickly become a nuisance, especially when it deletes the things you have to fill in.

Despite these issues, I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it for the price. It only takes around 3 to 4 hours to finish, but it has multiple endings. A new game plus mode exists, which fast-forwards the conversations. I wish it would skip the puzzles as well, so you can just focus on the endings, but alas, it is what it is.

review_text_raw:
A short supernatural investigative game that involves interacting with a cell phone which was left for you to find. You are given the task of finding out what happened to a girl named Anna whose phone you are now in possesion of. You investigate by interacting with individuals in her social media, dating app, email, phone contacts, and other media. Mostly you will choose from a pre-defined list of responses and actions, but there is some free play at times. 

There is a small puzzle element in that you need to "decrypt" her scrambled photos and text messages but it's fairly minor and doesn't really add anything to the experience. 

I have no idea if this was a mobile game first, but it does seem pretty ideal to be a mobile title. It still plays well on PC, but you'll be staring at the image of a phone 95% of the time. I use a dual monitor setup with my left monitor in portrait and my right in landscape so this was ideal to play on the portrait monitor while multitasking. 

I generally do not enjoy point and click, visual novel, or horror themed games and I would probably not place this game in any of those categories. There are some small horror elements which amount to a couple creepy photos and some creepy sound effects, but they're minimal. 

I received this as part of the humble bundle monthly subscription. I otherwise probably would have never purchased this game due to the misleading tags in Steam, but if I had paid the full price at the time of this review, I would have have regretted the purchase. I'll likely buy and play the sequel shortly. 

I found this very similar to Orwell, so would recommend it for fans of that title.

review_text_raw:
A story about an idiot surrounded by other idiots who sound like idiots.

At no point was there any reason to sympathize with Anna and her lifetime of bad decisions that got her into this mess. She's like the stereotypical white person in a horror movie whose phone suddenly goes to static and runs out of gas in the middle of the night in front of an obviously haunted house and says "I should investigate this immediately, and by myself!". Her dumbass ex, her dumbass new lover, her dumbass "best friend", all of whom supposedly want to help her yet they somehow form the main obstacles to doing so, especially the "best friend" who is basically a secondary antagonist for all the help she is. Aside from bit players like the completely unconvincing cop. I thought the cop was lying about being a cop and that that was important as first, but nope, just terrible voice acting, we're supposed to believe that's what cops sound like. Though he's not as bad as the villain revealed at the end, who sounds like a 13 year old boy who got his big brother to install voice changing software for him because he thinks it'll make him sound badass on voice chat while playing Halo. It's that bad. Was it supposed to be intimidating? Was it supposed to be a shocking reveal? It wasn't, just the annoying end to a nonsensical story about thoroughly unsympathetic idiots. Nothing about this is redeemable, this was a waste of a Humble Bundle pick. And they had the nerve to release a sequel? Why, because they can churn out terrible games like this once a week? I hope it at least has an "everyone dies" ending, because after meeting all of these characters, I honestly don't want any of them to live, it would be better for society for every one of them to go away.

review_text_raw:
An unsettling narrative that employs our intuitive knowledge of phones as a framework for oddly intuitive deductions and uncanny subversions.

It’s not a wholly unique concept for horror, but plenty of what’s done through interaction distinguishes Simulacra from the other cursed-PC or texting-based games with an opinion about digital privacy. Even if my thoughts were first drawn to comparisons, the strength of that initial ambiguity set within the benign familiarity of a mobile OS had me playing along in no time.

While the fixation on relationship drama does drive the story, it also seems to conflict with Simulacra's insidious tone. Although, the seemingly necessary overindulgence in others’ personal affairs does heighten a different sense of uneasiness. When the pixels aren't going "boo", Simulacra can be immensely unnerving. Silent realizations even provoked chills on more than one occasion.

Even if the narrative isn't unexpectedly divergent, the amount of time I spent mulling over the game's events speaks to the impact that they had on my participation. There's a lot to unwrap here and no better way to learn more than to play it for yourself.

review_text_raw:
[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

review_text_raw:
Not the worst but I am surprised at how highly rated this was.
I didn't find it overly scary beyond a few jump scares.  The most believable characters in the game are Anna and her friend, I enjoyed their realistic sideconversations more than most others in this game.  The other 2 main characters were overhammed to the point of ridiculousness which was very jarring altogether.
The game gears and mechanisms running under the phone UI were just a little bit too visible to be believable.  As I found certain conversations softlocked at random points until you hit some other arbitrary checkpoint which unlocked the rest of the thread.  Also some things were just not implemented well.  In what world is a job interview carried out over text?  And every phone call was completely one-sided which was so strange - I don't know why they didn't let you select responses like in the written conversations.
Speaking of dialogue, I didn't feel I had great freedom of choice in responding in conversations - I felt I was always fighting with what I was allowed to say.  And the ending fell rather flat, with a certain character taking a complete 180 degree change in attitude and outlook just so the ending could be tied off in a semi-neat bow.
I do have the second game in the series as I got it in a bundle, and the game wasn't so awful as to put me off trying it, so I will see if these devs have taken on board lessons learned and improved things in the second go round, but this game as it stands I would not recommend it.

Played the studio's other game "Sara Is Missing" on mobile and kept seeing this game recommended, so I got it during a Steam sale. Pretty similar to Sara is Missing, but I really enjoy the format of these games, and was hooked in just as much as that game. Simulacra is really well done, albeit somewhat campy (adds to the charm) and there are some typos, though that could be on purpose... nobody has perfect spelling when texting.

The writing is clever, and it is indeed an unsettling game at times. If you're into text adventures, whodunit, FMV horror, etc. with multiple endings and lots of branching paths, you'll definitely enjoy it. If it's not on sale, I'd probably recommend the mobile version to add to the immersion. Playing it on my PC wasn't quite as satisfying as it would have been on a phone.

review_text_raw: Creepy af. Very intuitive UI. Engaging storyline. Very immersive with headphones on and the lights off. Probably not the scariest thing you've ever played, but it's plenty suspenseful and even has a few jumpscare moments. Very cool the way they made it so that you play the entire game looking at the virtual screen of this virtual phone you discovered mysteriously. That's it, that's all the gameplay is, sending "texts", reading "emails", watching "videos"...all while trying to determine literally everything about this person who the phone belongs to, as well as determining what exactly is going on with the mysterious antagonist of the game. All in all, well worth the price, and the time spent playing. I made it thru one full playthru in 7 hours, but at least 2-3 of those hours was me walking away for awhile and coming back fresh.

The plot of this game is basically: 
you find a phone. The owner is apparently missing, and you check her phone in order to find her and what happened to her.

The idea sounds interesting on the paper. In reality, it's not well executed. Game isn't really good. 
1. The people you interact with. They are supposed to be in their 20's/30's... but they behave like 10 years old (especially Taylor and Greg... ). Most of the jokes are kinda lame too.
2. The acting is not that good either. 
3. The only decent thing in this game is maybe the "scary" elements, which don't happen often. 
Sometimes you can hear a voice whispering in your ear, I guess this is used to create some scare jump situation. This could be an interesting feature, however your character doesn't react at all to it. So... there is hardly any point to it. It's kinda out of place 

I heard that the second game is much better...

if you want some good games in which you interact with people using a phone/chat, you should instead try the game serie "Emilie Is Away" (the first game is free on Steam).

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a special and different game, i could say it a simulator/visual novel through a phone. In the begging, you found a mobile phone, that a girl lost but she also went missing. As you keep trying to find the girl, the story is going weirder and weirder( in a good way).It have a lot of texting and reading, so you can fill the gaps. The good thing is that all the reading is more like a chat so it flows smoothly. The game have a lot of endings, and after you beat it for the 1st time it unlocks the Begin+ mode, so you can go faster through the same texts. I try to get every ending and it took me around 6 hours. The background sound was a nice touch. Something that i found as con was that there is only 1 save and not multiple, so you can load and get faster some endings. Overall, i was suprised from this game in a very good way and i am gonna play the second game for sure

Το Simulacra είναι ένα ιδιαίτερο και διαφορετικό παιχνίδι, θα το χαρακτήριζα ως simulator/ visual novel μέσα από κινητό. Προσπαθείς να εντοπίσεις αυτό το άτομο για να του επιστρέψεις το κινητό αλλά στη πορεία εξελίσσεται σε μια ιδιαίτερα και περίεργη ιστορία. Ευχάριστη έκπληξη και σίγουρα θα δοκιμάσω και το δεύτερο παιχνίδι.

Found the premise interesting but the execution was barely tolerable.

Most of the characters are parody level awful, behave like bratty children and are entirely unlikable. The story line is agonizingly predictable and it feels like you spend too much of it waiting for the dialogue to catch up with you and navigating insufferable conversations without any way to move things along.

Rather than being a mystery to solve using a found phone and your wits, it's an on-rails idiot simulator that requires unintuitive decision making centred around not being mean to a dating app creep to succeed.

The platform is there for an interesting game but if I could take the time back I would, the moment the game seemed like it was finally going to get interesting, it ended.

review_text_raw:
I got this game today and I was incredibly excited to play. I did around 4 playthroughs, trying to see the easter eggs and gather all the achievements and overall I'm rather amazed.

The use of real people in a game was a new concept to me but I enjoyed the idea a lot, especially since it highlighted the possible dangers of the digital world and made them more transferrable to the real world. The voice acting was a bit unrealistic sometimes but that's a minor issue. 

There are 5 possible endings (though the game at the end shows you only four of them) and your choices really impact them. The dialogue options that the game revolves around either make or break your case, so you have to think about what to choose.

The game is rather easy, in most cases if you get stuck at anything either of the two characters that you keep talking to will help you. 

After over 6 hours of playthrough, I have to say I am really impressed with this game. It was my first time ever playing something of this format and I will now have expectations for the future. I would not count this game as a horror, since the repeated jumpscares and glitches were far from scary (but maybe they might scare some people, who knows!). The true scary theme in the game is the realization that people on the Internet might really be bad and you shouldn't trust everyone you meet online. 

Even though it's common knowledge, when showcased like this, it can be eye-opening to some. Great game.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra wasn't an entirely bad experience. I actually had a decent time with most of the game. However, the overall package is important to me with a game. I only played through Mass Effect 3 once because the endings were so off-putting that I did not have any interest in playing through again because the conclusion lowered the quality of the game as a whole for me. Mind you, Simulacra doesn't have two games that came before it to ruin the legacy of or anything, nor is it even a tenth the length of Mass Effect 3, but an unsatisfying conclusion to any heavily story-focused game is often the ruin of many a game that were doing well up until that point.

With Simulacra, you navigate a missing girl's cell phone, using the text messaging, web browser, social media posts, and a dating app to further your investigation into where the girl is, gain a couple of allies to help with said investigation, and ultimately conclude with a villain which I won't spoil the identity of or anything like that. I will say that you should be able to easily understand a great villain when the villain monologues to you about why said villain is doing things, and there should be some logical explanations for the reasoning for the villain's actions, etc. Also, a villain shouldn't just pop out of nowhere, typically. Imagine if you got to the end of a deep storyline, and suddenly an extraterrestrial pops out without proper foreshadowing. It would make for a "good bad movie," but a terrible plot point. Again, I won't say specifics about this villain, but the villain does not seem to have a very logical viewpoint, and the villain pops practically out of nowhere and can do things that the game never explains which are vital to the main storyline.

Finally, there appear to be four different endings. Apparently the game locks you out of certain endings based on certain actions you take at some point in the game. I have no idea what those actions were or when they came up. Worse yet, there is no manual saving in Simulacra. There is ONE autosave file that overwrites every time you complete an objective, meaning to see the other endings, you have to start the game from the beginning again. The text messages pop up faster than before, but the game still takes too long for me to have the patience to play through it again, especially since the gameplay wasn't particularly enjoyable for me. Simulating a real cell phone was a cool premise, but it wasn't "fun" to interact with for me outside of the initial surprises of what the very small cast of characters (and an even smaller cast of *relevant* characters) have to say.

The ending I got was horribly dark and unpleasant, and the other ending that was offered to me was clearly going to be horribly dark and unpleasant as well. Dark endings can be entertaining if the storyline gives a satisfying quality to them that doesn't leave you feeling cheated. In Simulacra, the villain effectively tells you "lulz, you made decisions (that I'm not going to specify which ones or when) which set this stuff up. Now make horrible choice A, or horrible choice B." I stopped caring about the story immediately upon being given these options, and just proceeded to the ending knowing my conclusion was going to suck because I didn't play with a walkthrough and the game doesn't allow saving aside from the regularly-overwriting autosave, so you can't just load back a few minutes to make a different decision and see things play out differently.

Without very clear points of making relevant decisions, and without a manual save you can load, AND without enjoyable dark/"bad" endings, Simulacra left me disappointed in what initially seemed like a game I was going to talk about to others and say great things about it, but walling off endings sneakily and overwriting autosaves without a manual save option ruined the overall package of this game for me. review_text_raw:
This was my first "found phone" type of mystery/horror to play so I was quite intrigued by the concept and mechanics as a whole. It really challenged how well of a snoop you were sometimes. Hilariously, I kept getting all the bad choices that ultimately led me to getting probably the worst ending possible and I wasn't really upset by that. However, there were some aspects that were a bit troubling for me throughout my playthrough. 

The jumpscares were considerably louder than the rest of the game and there are no audio options available. I guess I could understand if that was intentional since the "investigation" periods are very quiet (aside from [spoiler]the random knocks which were genuinely terrifying because I thought they were happening IRL[/spoiler]), but I actually did have fun just snooping through/messing with Anna's phone and texting everyone, so the cheap jumpscares took me out of the game pretty often.

Also, the climax (and the ending as a whole) just didn't totally sit right with me for some reason. Maybe my focus was waning by that point, but with hardly enough exposition to help drive the antagonist's motives, it just felt very out of left field. (Okay, maybe if I hadn't gone into this game ≈99% blind and maybe had also known [spoiler]what a simulacrum was[/spoiler], I would've had a better idea of what I was getting myself into.) With all that being said, I was left feeling underwhelmed and unsatisfied.

At the end of the day, SIMULACRA was [b]just okay[/b]. It's already very cheap in price, but I recommend you buy it during a sale if you're really that interested. I have just a small shred of hope for improvement on the second game.

Thanks, you kntz, are ya paying for the hearing aid I'm going to need after this introduction to your POS software? GREAT choice guys, leave the game's audio quality in the hands of the people that brought us Windows ME, Vista, 8 and 10. *slowclap*

Pretty cool mystery puzzle game, quite similar to Pony Island but not as good. The puzzles are creative enough, and the story is well-written and suspenseful – except for the finale when they decide to explain everything and then it goes downhill. The weakest content are the video segments; Anna is fine most of the time but the Taylor guy is a bad actor and some other voiceovers are pretty weak too.

Despite having multiple endings, the game has almost no replayability. The game is strictly linear and although you can speed up the text on your second playthrough, it's still tedious as hell to click through all those identical texts and puzzles just to see another ending. Play through the game once and then forget about it.

review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/glveJEYQO9M?t=792

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.
